Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Defense Minister Boris Pistorius talks security in Poland
- Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
- UniCredit and Germany reach Commerzbank takeover agreement
Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from Germany on Thursday, November 19:
German defense minister call Auschwitz a 'warning' to all of us
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Thursday called on Europeans to be vigilant against far-right extremism and warned of divisions and labels in society.
Speaking during a visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau, a former concentration camp, Pistorius said the site bore witness to the worst of Nazi Germany's crimes, calling it an absolute low point.
"It all started with defining what made a life unworthy; by dividing according to race, origin, faith, sexual orientation," Pistorius warned, saying that such marginalization was experiencing a "renaissance" and "gaining ground with far-right extremist parties across Europe."
The defense minister said Auschwitz provides all people, but particularly Germans, with a "symbol warning that we all bear responsibility for what happens and what must not be allowed to happen."
During his tour of the camp, Pistorius laid a wreath at its death wall, where Nazi soldiers shot roughly 5,000 prisoners dead, and lit a candle at the victims' memorial.
Before he departed the site, Pistorius expressed his wish that more German students and travel groups would visit the camp "than appears to be the case at present."
AfD politician accuses Le Pen of abandoning party 'core'
The deputy chairman of Germany's right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) has accused French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen of deserting her core values in her bid to achieve wider popularity and improve her chance of victory in French presidential elections.
For years, Le Pen claimed to be embarking on a policy of what's often called "de-demonization," trying to shed the extreme-right image of her father and predecessor, Jean-Marie Le Pen, and soften the stance of the party now called the National Rally or RN.
"Mrs. Le Pen, whom we all once admired greatly, now seems to have one fundamental principle: I say whatever the polls demand of me," Sven Tristschler told the right-leaning website The Pioneer.
France is headed into the last months of a presidential election campaign, with incumbent Emmanuel Macron's second and final term coming to an end and no clear candidate emerging as a main challenger to Le Pen as yet.
"At the end of the day, her victory would likely be even more catastrophic for the right than her defeat," Tritscher asserted. "The citizens would think they were voting to the right, only to get another Macron in the end."
He said that in hindsight, he was glad the AfD and RN parties had fallen out in European politics in recent years, and said AfD supporters should not anticipate a similar move toward moderation.
"A hollowing-out will not take place with us," he said, using the German scientific term for enucleation, the removal of the internal nucleus or core of a cell.
The AfD has made similar complaints about Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, accusing her party of a process of "Melonization" involving a softening of its core policy stances in a bid to retain power.
A similar power struggle is thought to be brewing within the AfD itself as it remains far adrift of majority support despite regularly polling as the largest single party in Germany at present.
Bundesbank expects inflation to rise in 2027
Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, said in its monthly report that inflation in Germany will rise "sharply" at the beginning of 2027.
Inflation could remain stable through the end of the year, given that a fuel tax cut is still keeping a lid on prices.
Inflation had fallen to 2.9% from 3.3% in September after the German government introduced the fuel discount.
But the central bank said the expiration of that fuel tax cut, along with other government measures, would drive inflation higher.
The report also highlighted that natural gas prices are expected to rise.
"On top of this, higher energy and input costs are expected to gradually feed through into the prices of other goods and certain services," the Bundesbank said.
Deutche Telekom to invest in French AI company
German telecommunications firm, Deutsche Telekom, announced that it will invest €100 million ($109.75 million) in French start-up Mistral AI, Europe's largest artificial intelligence company.
The investment will pour into Mistral from Telekom's subsidiary T.Capital Tech Fund.
Telekom said the move is a first step toward a strategic partnership, where the two firms plan to jointly support companies and the public sector in Germany in introducing tailored AI.
"Europe’s competitiveness depends on our ability to develop and use powerful AI," Telekom board member Ferri Abolhassan said in a statement announcing the deal. "Businesses must be able to trust this technology while retaining control over their data."
The move is the latest investment by Telekom in the AI space. In February, Telekom built an AI factory in Munich, which has since been expanded due to high demand.
Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Berlin for a summit of the "Coalition of the Willing." The group, which represents Kyiv's allies, is expected to push for a deeper European role in any efforts to end the war.
The process has so far been dominated by the US, Russia and Ukraine.
Zelenskyy wrote on X that "we are doing everything we can to ensure that Europe's presence in the negotiation process is fully represented."
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff flew to Germany to attend the summit at the Chancellery.

items.text:
Iraq's risky standoff: Government vs. Iran-allied militias
November 19, 2026
For years, there have all kinds of rumors about Jurf al-Sakhar, an area around 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It is controlled by an Iraqi militia called Kataib Hezbollah, that's closely allied with Iran, and no Iraqi government troops or news media outlets have been allowed inside for around 12 years.
Rumors about what's happening in the area include allegations about secret prisons, mass graves, drone and weapons manufacturing and storage, as well as criminal activity such as oil smuggling. Jurf al-Sakhar is also allegedly a base for foreign, Hezbollah-supporting nationals from Iran, Yemen, Bahrain and Lebanon.
Recently two people — an Israeli researcherand a US journalist — who were kidnapped by an Iraqi militia are thought to have been held captive in this area.
Jurf al-Sakhar previously had an estimated 89,000 residents but after the extremist group known as the "Islamic State," or IS, rose to power in Iraq in 2014, much of the population was displaced in fighting. The area was eventually taken over by Kataib Hezbollah, a militia that had fought IS alongside other armed groups.
As a collective, the armed groups are referred to as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF. Not all of them have pledged allegiance to Iran but Kataib Hezbollah, a Shiite Muslim majority group, has.
In the past 12 years, tens of thousands of the displaced people from here, mostly Sunni Muslims, have not been allowed to return and the area has been described as militarized.
Its name was even changed by Kataib Hezbollah fighters, from Jurf al-Sakhar ("rocky bank") to Jurf al-Nasr ("bank of victory").
'Not even over our dead bodies'
But recent events may shake Kataib Hezbollah's hold on this area.
An early November report for the Iraqi government says that since 2021, the group has smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, siphoned from pipelines around Jurf al-Sakhar.
Kataib Hezbollah denies this.
Iraq's new government, headed by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, made several arrests based on the report and demanded that Kataib Hezbollah leave Jurf al-Sakhar by Friday, Nov. 20.
Kataib Hezbollah rejected al-Zaidi's ultimatum, with a spokesperson saying the group would not withdraw "not even over our dead bodies."
Al-Zaidi then ordered state security forces to surround the area, while Hezbollah reportedly brought in reinforcements.
Observers have described the standoff as one of the most consequential and riskiest confrontations between an Iraqi government and Iranian-backed militiasin Iraq in more than two decades.
"It is a political signal that things will change, that he [al-Zaidi] wants to disarm militias, integrate them into state and claim back the state's authority," Ulf Laessing, head of the Syria and Iraq project for Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, or KAS, told DW. "But it's a minefield and he needs to navigate carefully."
The standoff is also the result of long-running political tensions in Iraq, where the state is torn between its US allies on the one hand and Iranian allies on the other. Both hold sway in Iraq and are considered important relationships.
During Donald Trump's presidency of the US, and thanks to the US and Israel's war with Iran, there's been more pressure on Iraq to disarm Iran's allies inside the country. Al-Zaidi has set a deadline of next June to bring all weapons under the state's control.
Tensions, fears grow
The situation in Jurf al-Sakhar became even more tense this week. Al-Zaidi announced a new security plan for the area that involves other members of the PMF, state security forces and the police. Kataib Hezbollah rejected the plan.
"Al-Zaidi appears serious about ending Kataib Hezbollah's autonomous control of Jurf al-Sakhar," Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW. "Deploying federal forces and now establishing a new security command there shows this has moved beyond rhetoric."
But how dangerous is Kataib Hezbollah really? After all, al-Zaidi was actually nominated for the prime minister's job by a political bloc known as the Coalition Framework, or CF — these are the politicians who represent the PMF in parliament. Kataib Hezbollah's political party, Harakat Huqooq, is part of the CF.
And other researchers have been critical on social media, noting that the PMF troops that will be given partial control over Jurf al-Sakhar (should Kataib Hezbollah withdraw) are associated with that group anyway.
But Iraqi news media have also reported that there are divisions inside the CF, and apparently even within Kataib Hezbollah, about how to deal with the current standoff. Reportedly, some senior officials think that parts of Jurf al-Sakhar could be handed to federal forces in a gradual withdrawal, the London-based outlet Amwaj Media reported earlier this week, while some senior members of Kataib Hezbollah would seemingly prefer to hand the territory over to certain PMF brigades rather than to state security forces.
What will happen next?
Late Thursday afternoon, the news agency Reuters reported that, according to three anonymous officials, all parties had come to an agreement that would allow government forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.
A compromise is good because it avoids violence, KAS' Laessing said. "It might not be what al-Zaidi initially hoped for but it's still a political signal."
If it did come to actual fighting, the Iraqi military has more resources than Kataib Hezbollah, al-Shakeri explained. "[It] could probably take Jurf al-Sakhar if the political leadership and security institutions remained united," he said. "But there would be no easy victory. Kataib Hezbollah does not need to defeat the Iraqi army conventionally. It can impose costs through asymmetric attacks, political pressure and its networks inside the state."

Sutton's predictions v world champion boxer Lauren Price
- Published
Manchester United start life under new boss Mauricio Pochettino on Sunday but will they get their first Premier League win since August when they face Liverpool at Anfield?
"My worry for United is that they have one of the worst back fours in the Premier League," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.
"Their defensive record is something Pochettino will try to address but, whoever he picks, they are just not very good."
Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers anad a variety of guests.
For week 11, he takes on boxer Lauren Price, who is an Arsenal fan.
She will defend her unified welterweight titles against Michaela Kotaskova on Friday, and has a shot at becoming Wales' first undisputed world champion after the vacant WBO welterweight title was added to the fight.
Price returns to home soil at the Utilita Arena in Cardiff for a fight that will be shown live on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer, from 21:00 GMT.
Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.
The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.
A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.
Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.
Before turning to boxing, Price was a world kickboxing champion and international footballer - she captained the Wales Under-19 side, and played for the senior team as well as Cardiff City.
"My football days have helped me massively to get where I am in the ring today," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport.
"I honestly believe my footwork, and how fast my feet are, comes from when I played football.
"I am really proud of everything I achieved in football, especially playing for my country. It is the same now in boxing - to get in the ring and represent Wales is always an honour."
Price said the support of her grandparents helped her become successful at so many sports - and she followed her grandad, Derek, by becoming an Arsenal fan too.
"When I was a kid I was absolutely besotted with football and Arsenal were THE team when I was growing up," she explained.
"It was just the way they played under Arsene Wenger, and how they passed the ball - it was incredible. I loved Robin van Persie but Thierry Henry was my icon, my hero."
Chris Sutton and Lauren Price were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.
The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

In contrast, Fulham's results have improved of late and they are unbeaten in four league games. They've done all right whenever I've seen them this season, so I'm not surprised to see them picking up points.
Still, the international break probably came at a good time for Maresca to sort things out. Erling Haaland is scoring again too - not that he ever really stopped for very long - and I'm expecting City to be much better here.
I'm even going for them to keep a clean sheet, for the first time in eight games. I'm always brave... which is why I am bottom of the predictions table.
Sutton's prediction: 2-0
Lauren's prediction: City are having a tricky time of it at the moment but they should still win this. 2-0
AI's prediction: 3-1
- Villa Park, 15:00
I was at Sunderland's win over Chelsea and they thoroughly deserved it. They had been on a dreadful run of results before then, but it was a reminder of what they are about.
Brian Brobbey was just phenomenal for the Black Cats in that game but, like his captain Granit Xhaka, he is injured and will miss out here.
That just makes me think Aston Villa will have the edge. I always fancy them at home anyway with the way they go after teams, although I don't think this will be easy for them.
Villa boss Unai Emery was fuming after his side threw away a two-goal lead twice in their 4-4 draw at Manchester United, but they will hold on this time while Sunderland go down fighting.
Sutton's prediction: 2-1
Lauren's prediction: Villa are going really well. 2-1
AI's prediction: 2-0

Bournemouth have won eight games in a row in all competitions and it is incredible how Marco Rose has turned things around after a slow start.
The Cherries were absolutely flying before the international break - but will the two weeks off affect their momentum?
Forest did not need the break either, after their brilliant win over Manchester City.
That was such an important result for their manager Oliver Glasner but I think they will find it difficult to follow it up at Bournemouth.
Sutton's prediction: 2-1
Lauren's prediction: Forest shocked City last time out but I am going with Bournemouth here, they are on a brilliant run. 2-1

items.text:
Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
- Published
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.
Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.
Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.
"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.
"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.
"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."
The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.
Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."
Manchester United have declined to comment.
Did we learn anything?
There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.
While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbuemo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, while neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season.
On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'Rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.
Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.
The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.
Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

items.text:
European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Ukraine's main European allies met in Berlin for 'Coalition of the Willing' talks
- Leaders of Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy gathered following talks involving President Donald Trump, Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in China
- US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were also at the meeting to brief allies about discussions in China
- Ukraine's European allies are pushing to be included in US-backed negotiations with Russia
Follow the latest on Thursday, 19th November, below:
Message of European unity 'relayed to President Trump' — Jared Kushner
US special envoy Jared Kushner said unity in Europe was clear in the talks and that support for Ukraine remained strong.
"What we came away from today with is really seeing that Europe is very united and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine," Kushner said. "We relayed this to President Trump."
Kushner said this would also be relayed to the Russian delegation and that there was "a real desire for peace."
Kushner said that Trump had joined the Berlin meeting by phone and provided an update on the talks in Shenzhen with President Putin and President Xi.
"He sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage with both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said.
Kushner told reporters the talks with European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "made a lot of progress on what those security guarantees can look like," as well as a post-war prosperity plan.
He also said Russia was "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war.
Macron says question of Ukraine's NATO accession should be reopened
French President Emmanuel Macron said that amid Russia's continued attacks on infrastructure and "maximalist demands," the first priority was for Ukraine to be able to defend itself.
Macron said allies needed to ensure that Ukraine had everything it needed to resist and defend itself from Russian attacks.
"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," Macron said in Berlin.
"Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now," the French leader insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Macron said security guarantees were a "key element for our long-term negotiations" and the security plan it had already submitted should remain.
Zelenskyy says next round of talks must include Europe
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Europe should be part of talks going forward.
"America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation at the negotiations is necessary," Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said his country needed international support ahead of another winter and added that more work was needed to "push Russia to be more constructive in any negotiations."
He also said much work was done to make the Berlin meeting "as concrete as possible."
Zelenskyy thanked all partners and expressed gratitude to Germany, France, the UK, the US along with those who had come out in support of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy highlighted the importance of air defense and said that Russia's aerial bombardments were steadily intensifying.
Zelenskyy said there was no sign this would change as "the Russians have rejected every single proposal for de-escalation."
Zelenskyy said that it was "crucial" that the US "exerts influence on Russia."
Merz pushes for European representation in peace talks
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for Europe to play a role in helping secure peace in the war in Ukraine.
"Today we prepared for ourselves for possible peace talks," Merz said.
"These talks should comprise Ukraine, Russia, the United States and Europe," Merz said, adding that this format offered the best chance of securing peace.
The German leader said Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy would speak on behalf of Europe.
He went on to call the trilateral talks between the president of the United States, Russia and China today at an APEC summit a "photo op" and said such a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine.
Merz pledged "powerful support" for Ukraine in 2027 and mentioned the €45 billion earmarked for next year by the European Commission.
Merz said the level of support was being provided in order for Ukraine to be able to protect itself and that allies wanted the war to end.
Outcome of Ukraine war will 'shape security in Europe' — Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the future of European security would be molded by what was happening in Ukraine.
"The outcome of this war will shape security in Europe for a long time to come," Merz said in a post on social media platform X.
"Together with our partners, we continue our support for peace in Ukraine. That's why we came together today for the Coalition of the Willing," Merz said.
He accompanied his comments with pictures from roundtable talks of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin.
Zelenskyy says he discussed 'key issues' with German, French and British leaders
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he went over "key issues and needs" with German, French and British leaders.
Zelenskyy shared a video on X of his meeting with France's Emmanuel Macron, Britain's Andy Burnham and Germany's Friedrich Merz.
He said they discussed "countering Russian shahed drones and missiles, protecting the energy sector and infrastructure, as well as the diplomatic efforts."
"It is important that today's Coalition of the Willing meeting and bilateral meetings with leaders deliver results," he added.

items.text:
The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.
She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."
It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)
As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?
David and Nina's Four L's
When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:
Love. "You gotta love each other."
Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."
Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.
Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.
The Magic Six
I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.
Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?
The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.
Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.
Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.
Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.
Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.
Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.
Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.
State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.
Listen. Don't Fix.
Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.
"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.
Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."
It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.
Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.
Find Your Rhythm
Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?
Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.
As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."
So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."
For more, follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

items.text:
Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use, meaning it can help you “get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” the company says. Google suggests the feature might be useful for things like speeding up workflows, filling in forms, making presentations, and listing items for sale.
Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
With the new computer use feature, Google says Gemini can better help with things like filling in forms and creative workflows.
Users will be able to decide which of your apps Gemini can access, and be able to follow along as Gemini works because it has its own background window that shows a live preview in your chat, Google says. The feature is rolling out now in English for users in the US.
Gemini is introducing the new feature ahead of Apple launching new restrictions for apps wanting “full disk access” on Mac due to potential risks from AI agents with computer use. A preview of the settings rolled out with this week’s macOS 27.3 beta.

Iraq’s prime minister says security forces will establish a joint operations centre in the town of Jurf al-Sakhar, in a com
items.text:
Iraq reaches compromise with Kataib Hezbollah over armed group stronghold
The compromise reached will station forces that include brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces.
Iraq’s prime minister says security forces will establish a joint operations centre in the town of Jurf al-Sakhar, in a compromise with the Iranian-backed Kataib Hezbollah armed group over control of a strategic area south of Baghdad.
The Jurf al-Sakhar area has long been a stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah, and the new agreement comes after the Iraqi government announced plans to send in security forces amid allegations that Kataib Hezbollah was smuggling oil.
The compromise reached late on Thursday will see a new combined force deployed to the area, consisting of a brigade from the Iraqi Army, a brigade from the Federal Police, a regiment from the Energy Police to provide protection for oil pipelines in the area, and two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are officially part of Iraq’s security forces, including some Kataib Hezbollah fighters.
In a statement, Iraq’s armed forces commander-in-chief said the new joint operations centre will open at 6am local time (03:00 GMT) on Friday morning.
A senior Iraqi official previously told Al Jazeera that Kataib Hezbollah had until Friday to leave Jurf al-Sakhar. The group had threatened to confront government troops, and had rejected the government’s efforts to disarm non-state militias.
Earlier in the week, an Iraqi official also told Al Jazeera that the commander of the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, arrived in Iraq to push for a solution due to the simmering tensions with Iran.

items.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
items.summary:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other le
items.text:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.
Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September, which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.
Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.
As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.
Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.
The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

Rules designed to safeguard media pluralism during elections campaigns will apply to France's most influential YouTubers in the run-up to next year's presidential contest, media regulator Arcom warned on Thursday
items.text:
French media regulator says it will monitor top YouTubers for bias in election coverage
Rules designed to safeguard media pluralism during elections campaigns will apply to France's most influential YouTubers in the run-up to next year's presidential contest, media regulator Arcom warned on Thursday, reflecting the growing influence of content creators whose audiences often outstrip those of traditional media companies.
France's media regulator announced Thursday that it will monitor online influencers and content creators for political bias in the run-up to presidential elections next year, in a major expansion of its powers.
Arcom takes on a key role in French election campaigns, ensuring news channels and radio stations offer airtime for all presidential candidates or parties running for office.
The change reflects the growing influence of YouTubers and other content creators whose audiences, particularly of young people, are sometimes bigger than traditional media companies.
"There's a new phenomenon, it's here and it's massive," Arcom president Martin Ajdari announced at a press conference in Paris.
France heads to the polls on April 18 and May 2 to elect a new president, with far-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leading in the polls, followed by Gen Z favourite Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Read moreFrench presidential election: How far-left Mélenchon became a Gen Z favourite
Parliamentary elections will follow, probably in June.
Under Arcom's rules, presidential candidates have to be given airtime relative to their projected score in the first phase of campaigning.
But from April 5-30, they have to be given equal treatment.
Ajdari stressed that Arcom would only monitor the most significant French video creators – such as HugoDecrypte or Guillaume Pley – and audio-only podcasters would not be concerned.
Current affairs YouTuber HugoDecrypte (real name Hugo Travers) has become "the single most important news source for younger audiences", reaching more than a quarter of all those under 35, according to research from the Reuters Institute think-tank.
Interview show host Guillaume Pley, who has already announced plans to speak with presidential candidates next year, has 3.8 million subscribers on YouTube
"This issue arises in very concrete terms for creators whose audiences exceed those of traditional television channels," Ajdari added.
France has been at the forefront of global efforts to regulate the online world, with legislation passed in 2023 establishing possible prison sentences and fines for influencers who fail to declare their paid promotions or advertise fraudulent products.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.summary:
Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?
November 19, 2026
Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military p
items.text:
Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?
November 19, 2026
Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Xi hailed the talks as "groundbreaking," saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.
The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.
Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.
The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.
While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were "positive, constructive and fruitful," Trump heralded the gathering as "really making history."
Who gained the most from the meeting?
For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as "he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world."
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.
The meeting itself is a "major outcome for Russia," he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as "reinforcing Russia's standing in the world."
Beijing reluctant to accept nuclear limits
The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.
Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.
But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.
Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.
Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms. "The gap between China's nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China's perspective, it doesn't seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area."
The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is "actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office."
"So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement," Lee said.
But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.
A reluctant host?
China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm Beijing's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.
Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.
But Beijing eventually "managed to get the outcome they wanted" and kept the European conflict out of the meeting's focus, she noted. "China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines," she added. "So, I think China probably came out feeling okay."
Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "second Yalta," referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.
That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.
In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a "joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."
But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan's Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison "is a bit of a stretch," given the vast differences between 1945 and now.
Will there be more such trilaterals?
Putin also said that all three leaders "agree that it's a useful format," and such meetings could take place again.
Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup "is unlikely to be just a one-off" and there will likely be more such meetings in the coming years. "Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia," he underlined.

items.summary:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.
In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages a
items.text:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.
In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.
One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app.
“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.
Meta did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

items.text:
What impact will the Shenzhen summit have on the US-China trade war?
Despite warm words between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen Thursday, the simmering trade war between Washington and Beijing still looks to be no closer to resolution.
Sometimes the meeting is the message.
The three-way talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Chinese tech capital of Shenzhen Thursday lasted all of 90 minutes.
Just what exactly the three men said to one another through their interpreters during that hour-and-a-half will remain a mystery.
Certainly, the joint “Declaration toward Peace” published afterwards by Beijing and Moscow gave little away: unspecified UN reforms, agreement to boost global oil production, a terse warning to the International Criminal Court and similar global bodies not to “abuse their jurisdiction” and a unanimous agreement that nuclear wars left no winners alive to celebrate.
Read moreHistoric trilateral summit live: Trump, Xi and Putin agree that a nuclear war must never be fought
While some watchers had warned not to expect any major announcements, others had raised fears that the historic meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum would be a new Yalta Conference.
About us, without us
The 1945 summit between the leaders of the allied Soviet Union, United States and Britain decided the shape of the global institutions that would rise out of the ashes of World War II and the fate of the eastern European countries following the defeat of Nazi Germany and its fascist allies.
With Russia’s brutal campaign in Ukraine dragging deeper into its fifth year, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky warned against a new meeting between the self-identified superpowers that threatened to once again divide the world up into discrete spheres of influence – regardless of the impact on the peoples who found the borders shifting beneath their feet.
While Beijing and Moscow had both brushed aside comparisons with the conference, the carefully orchestrated spectacle of Xi, Trump and Putin as a 21st-century incarnation of Yalta’s “Big Three” did much to drape the three men with the trappings of World War II-style "great powers".
But speaking to FRANCE 24 in the hours ahead of the meeting, Jean-François Di Meglio, steering committee chair of the Asia Centre think tank, said that parallels between Thursday’s talks and the discussions that ushered in the end of World War II didn’t stand up to scrutiny.
“The term ‘multipolarity’ is essential – and that’s why the comparison that’s often been made with Yalta doesn’t work,” he said. “Because there was a form of membership, a system where each participants’ differences were recognised … Whereas here, what matters most is China’s refusal in principle of a single world order under the aegis of common principles.”

Under the banner of multipolarity, China has for years championed a reworking of the international system that would give more weight to voices from the underdeveloped Global South – of which it has set itself up as an unofficial standard bearer.
Di Meglio said that China’s desire to overturn the Western hegemony that has reigned since the latter half of the 20th century should not be mistaken for altruism.
“While this multipolarity – which is being preached with a certain degree of opportunism, as we can see all too clearly in the way this meeting has been organised – is indeed China’s guiding principle, is it a sincere one or not? It is obvious that everything is being done in China’s best interest.”
A tenuous truce
Despite the warm words that Trump and Xi had for one another, the talks seem to have done little to resolve the simmering tensions between the two powers. Beijing’s threat last year to withhold critical rare earth exports won them a reprieve from Trump’s trade war, but the truce ends in January.
China has so far been one of the few countries to go toe-to-toe with the US after Trump unleashed a slew of tariffs against allies and adversaries alike, leveraging its unquestioned dominance in the rare earth and critical minerals supply chains that form the bedrock of the world’s cutting-edge technologies.
The US on Monday tightened rules around the export of advanced computing chips crucial for the development of frontier AI, an industry where US corporations still seem to hold an advantage over their Chinese rivals. The rules also restrict Chinese access to overseas data centres that would allow companies to access advanced computing power remotely.
With the Democrats having seized the House and Senate from Trump’s Republicans in the midterm elections earlier this month, Di Meglio said that foreign policy would become even more central to the president’s final two years in office.
“Artificial intelligence has raw materials, and those raw materials are rare earths,” he said. “And in Donald Trump’s mind, figuring out how to break this deadlock must be very, very high on his list of priorities.”

items.text:
‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
A week after a fizzled impeachment bid, analysts say Hegseth continues to face backlash for his leadership at Pentagon.
In the wake of the United States midterm elections, attention has turned to whether Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will be able to preserve his cabinet-level position once Congress’s new Democratic majorities are sworn in.
Already, the Fox News host-turned-military-chief has faced mounting calls for his removal from office.
But analysts question the extent to which Hegseth’s impeachment would affect military policy under President Donald Trump.
“Ultimately, the secretary of defence is a powerful participant in shaping a war,” said Jasmine El-Gamal, a former Middle East adviser in the Pentagon.
El-Gamal, however, believes targeting Hegseth alone would not be enough to secure accountability for decisions like launching the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hegseth holds significant power in directing the US war effort, she explained, but he also works hand-in-hand with the president and his advisers.
“Calling him merely an ‘executor’ understates that power, while calling him its sole architect understates the president’s power and obscures where particular decisions were actually made,” El-Gamal said.
Facing impeachment
Since he was sworn in on January 25, 2025, Hegseth has overseen some of Trump’s most controversial international campaigns, including the war on Iran and a series of deadly boat strikes in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.
Both campaigns have been accused of violating international law. The Iran war, in particular, became a political albatross for Trump’s Republican Party during the midterm race.
A poll earlier this month found that 44 percent of US voters said they were less likely to vote for a midterm candidate who supported the war.
That number dwarfed the 13 percent who said they were more inclined to vote for such a candidate, by a ratio of more than three to one.
The Democratic Party scored a thumping victory in the November 3 midterms, flipping both the House of Representatives and the Senate from Republican control.
Less than a week later, Hegseth faced a push for impeachment, led by outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie.
Among the eight articles of impeachment Massie filed were accusations that Hegseth had dismantled fundamental safeguards to protect civilian lives, leading to incidents like the bombing of an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed at least 120 children.
But the impeachment proceedings were shelved on November 10, after the Republicans’ lame-duck majority in the House voted 211 to 204 to block the measure. Eleven Democrats were absent for the vote.
Scrutiny of Pentagon chiefs
Hegseth is hardly the first Pentagon chief to face pressure to leave office following a dismal election for his party.
In November 2006, Republicans likewise suffered a midterm rout amid a groundswell of voter ire over the US-led wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Both chambers of Congress that year flipped to Democratic control.
Within a day of the vote, then-President George W Bush announced that his defence secretary, the late Donald Rumsfeld, would resign. He cited the Iraq war in his remarks.
“I recognise that many Americans voted last night to register their displeasure with the lack of progress being made there,” Bush said of the conflict.
Hegseth, however, has resisted calls for his resignation. In a five-minute video posted two days after the midterms, Hegseth dismissed his critics as “deep-state radicals” obsessed with “political theatre”.
“They attack us because we are effective. It’s not going to work. We will not back down,” Hegseth said. “We put America and the war-fighter first, always and without apology. And that fight continues in the lame-duck Congress.”
His message of defiance included an appeal for the military to “stay the course”, including in the war against Iran.
“I’ll assure you, we have only just begun to fight,” Hegseth added. “We are more determined than ever, more resolute than ever to finish what we have started.”
A key role in the war
Some of the criticism, however, has come from within Hegseth’s own party. Vice President JD Vance, for instance, said the “real reason” the Republicans lost the midterms is “obvious to almost everyone”.
“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on social media.
Hala Rharrit, a former US diplomat who spent 18 years in the State Department, was among the officials who resigned before Trump took office for his second term, in protest of the US involvement in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
She explained that Hegseth would have been critical in guiding some of the Iran war’s most divisive moments.
The bombing of the Minab elementary school, for example, took place on February 28, the first day of the conflict.
Rharrit said Hegseth and other senior Department of Defense (DOD) officials would have drawn up the initial strike lists before advising Trump on the targets for final approval.
“I suspect that Trump would not get into the granularities of which targets to strike on day one,” Rharrit told Al Jazeera.
“Hegseth and others in DOD had a lot to do with those precise decisions, which also runs through lawyers.”
She also drew a line between decisions taken by Hegseth and Trump and the losses the US and its allies have endured since the war began.
Iran has retaliated against US and Israeli attacks with strikes across the Middle East. At least 23 US service members have died in the conflict, and 865 were wounded.
“Ultimately, they are both responsible, not just for the strikes in Iran, but also for making American service members and diplomats throughout the region sitting ducks,” said Rharrit.
Congress reasserting its authority?

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – The Kenya Red Cross has strengthened its flood response capacity following the donation of 31 outboard boat engines by the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The organisation says the equipment will improve the ability of its emergency response teams and volunteers to conduct water rescues and deliver humanitarian assistance to communities affected by flooding.
In a statement on X, the Kenya Red Cross said heavy rains had already cut off some communities, citing the situation in Tana River.
It noted that the engines would help rescue teams reach stranded families faster, conduct search and rescue operations in floodwaters and transport relief supplies to areas where roads have become impassable.
The organisation expressed gratitude to the ICRC for supporting its emergency preparedness and response operations across the country.

items.summary:

items.text:
Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.
The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.
Everful is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year, about two and a half years after its launch, co-founder Sisi Song said. The company ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries and works with over 30,000 factory partners, she added. Its online wholesale catalog includes more than 20 million products.
Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous company to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.
Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.
The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.
“We take care of everything,” Han said. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”
Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.
Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.
Because Everful sources from Chinese factories, ongoing U.S.-China trade tensions and tariffs bear directly on its business. Song said the co-founders have been thinking about geopolitical issues since day one of building the company, and that this has shaped Everful’s strategy from the outset, leveraging her experience at Alibaba and Bessemer Venture Partners.
She mentioned the Trump administration’s suspension of the de minimis exemption, which had allowed eligible shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the U.S. duty-free, as one example of a shift in trade policy.
Song explained such changes could favor a model that combines overseas sourcing with local retail sales. “We’re empowering local retailers and brands,” she said. “Long-term cross-border commerce will be cross-border B2B sourcing plus local selling.”
Everful plans to use the Series A round to expand its presence in the U.S. and Europe, particularly the U.K., France, and Italy, while investing in AI to automate product customization and other sourcing workflows. It also aims to deepen integrations with e-commerce platforms, building on its Shopify integration as it works toward becoming an end-to-end infrastructure platform for global sourcing.
The startup employs about 70 full-time staff globally, including 45 in research and development. It has also established an AI operations team to connect engineering and business functions.

items.text:
Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz faces a deepening water crisis
Fuel shortages and the loss of access to wells have left residents dependent on unsafe water.
Taiz, Yemen – Qaid al-Sharaabi waited three days before it was his turn to receive a tanker of clean water.
But the delay is not the only problem. He says he now has to pay more – the result of the Houthi siege on Taiz, in southwestern Yemen.
“This is the second time since the siege began a month-and-a-half ago that I’ve had to pay twice the price for a water tanker,” al-Sharaabi told Al Jazeera. “I’m afraid that if things continue like this, more residents will resort to using unsafe water.”
The United Nations children’s agency (UNICEF) says that water production in Taiz has nearly halved, while more than 800,000 people are reported to be cut off from humanitarian assistance.
The crisis has left the city reeling, even as government soldiers try to defend it, in the latest round of fighting to hit the area since the war in Yemen started in 2014.
Hospital administrators are warning of a public health disaster, while government officials are unsure how much longer they will have the funds needed to carry out even limited services.
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, has long suffered from severe water shortages.
But, according to Wafiq al-Aghbari, director-general of Taiz governorate’s Local Water and Sanitation Corporation, the crisis “intensified in 2015, with the first siege imposed on the city by the Houthis, and continued to worsen year after year, as the suffering of the city’s residents grew”.
He said the crisis has deepened since the Houthis laid siege to the city again in October, after they made advances against government forces in the countryside around Taiz.
Before the war started in 2014, al-Aghbari explained, Taiz received about 20,000 cubic metres (700,000 cubic feet) of water per day from six large wellfields, which had supplied the city and its immediate surroundings for years.
But only one of those wellfields is inside the city limits, and before the war, it had only been used in emergencies.
By 2015, Taiz had lost access to all five of its external wellfields, which had either fallen under Houthi control or were on the front lines, leaving the city reliant on its emergency wells.
But work in the past few years to dig additional wells and rehabilitate existing sources had brought daily production capacity up to 5,000 cubic metres (175,000 cubic feet) – still just 14 percent of the city’s estimated daily needs.
Tightening siege
The Houthi encirclement of Taiz in October led to the Iranian-backed group seizing control of Hadhran al-Dhabab, an external wellfield that had been partially restored in August 2025.
The situation has led to the water corporation losing 3,200 cubic metres (112,000 cubic feet) of daily production capacity – 1,200 cubic metres (42,000 cubic feet) after pumping stopped from the Hadhran al-Dhabab wellfield, and a further 2,000 cubic metres (70,000 cubic feet) after wells inside the city stopped operating because of a shortage of diesel. The corporation is now able to produce only 1,800 cubic metres (63,180 cubic feet) a day from the emergency wells that it can still operate.
Al-Aghbari said the consequences of the siege had extended beyond the widening gap between water supplies and demand.
Funding and supplies for the city’s charitable water distribution points, known as “sabeel”, have also been disrupted, because of shortages of fuel and water.
According to al-Aghbari, the subsidised distribution points had previously provided up to 1.5 million litres (396,000 gallons) of fresh water a day, alongside a further 1 million litres (264,000 gallons) of untreated water.
“The water corporation has entered a major financial crisis as a result of the loss of most international and local funding for its operations, at a time when the corporation is also under immense pressure because of the growing shortfall in meeting local water needs,” al-Aghbari said.
He added that this was especially problematic because more residents cannot afford to buy commercially-supplied water as a result of the worsening economic situation, and become more dependent on the free water distribution points.
The owner of one commercial water tanker, who did not want to give his name for security reasons, said that prices had risen sharply at the beginning of the siege, from 18,000 riyals per tanker (about $12 at parallel market rates) to 30,000 riyals (about $20).
He continues to try to pick up water from the Hadhran al-Dhabab wellfield, but said that the process had become difficult.
“[That is] because of the consequences of the siege, including the inspection procedures imposed by the Houthi group … which last for hours,” he said. “Sometimes we are prevented from entering and remain outside the city for more than a day, on the grounds that there are risks because of heightened military and security tensions.”
The Houthis have denied responsibility for the closure of roads into Taiz. Human Rights Watch has said that residents, aid workers, and UN officials had blamed the armed group for shortages in the city.
Contaminated water
The consequences of the siege have gone beyond its humanitarian and economic impact, with serious implications for public health, according to Dr Abdulqawi al-Shamiri, the director of Taiz’s al-Taawun Hospital.
He warned of “serious health disasters because of the interruption of safe water supplies that residents used to obtain from groundwater fields outside the city”.
Al-Shamiri said water from the emergency wells within the city had “long been unfit for human use, as a large proportion of it has become contaminated, or is hard water containing high concentrations of salts”.
He explained that the contamination was the result of sewage mixing with water because of poorly maintained sewage networks, and rubbish dumped in streets and floodwater channels. The Houthis, al-Shamiri said, have prevented waste from

items.text:
Anthropic starts trading in the US after blockbuster IPO
Anthropic’s IPO surpasses SpaceX, marking the largest initial public offering in US history at $81bn.
Anthropic, the maker of Claude, is now trading on the Nasdaq through the largest initial public offering in history, surpassing the debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
The stock began trading on the ticker ANT midday on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence lab, valued at $2 trillion, said last week that it would offer 825 million shares with its IPO at a price range of $70 to $78 per share. However, that changed on Wednesday when the Dario Amodei-led company announced it would sell 980 million shares at $83 each.
By the time the stock ultimately went live, at 11:50am in New York (16:50 GMT), it was trading at $111.50 per share, a 34 percent rise.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 0.3 percent in midday trading while the Dow Jones Industrial Average by 0.9 and the S&P500 is down 0.2 percent.
The high-profile IPO has fuelled excitement across the board, including among industry insiders such as Michael Monaghan, founder and portfolio manager at Founders ETF.
“We have indicated our intention to buy in the IPO and hope to get an allocation. The books are well oversubscribed with high-quality orders, according to our trading counterparts,” he told Al Jazeera.
Anthropic’s listing is the first of the two major AI labs to go public on US markets, as competitor OpenAI has also eyed an IPO. However, it comes at a rocky time for the AI industry, amid the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia invested a combined $20bn in Anthropic, including $10bn in a partnership announced in November 2025 and another $10bn in a share purchase tied to its IPO.
The massive IPO also comes amid backlash from voters in the recently concluded midterm elections, where all but one ballot initiative restricted expansion of data centres, and a sweep by Democrats who ran on platforms of reining in the AI industry.
“Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain,” IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer told the Reuters news agency.
That has not dented analysts’ assessments of the sector.
“Anthropic’s IPO [is] a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director of Yorkville Ives, said in a note.
Anthropic is also closely watched for how intertwined it is with other tech companies, including Amazon and Google.
Anthropic has committed $110bn to Amazon for computing infrastructure over long-term agreements and at least $121.3bn to Google.
Underscored concerns
Anthropic’s Wall Street debut comes amid growing concerns about the safety of its technology. The company’s more than 300-page SEC filing devoted approximately 90 pages to outlining potential risks, including warnings that its AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.
The company also disclosed a net loss of $104bn in the first nine months of 2026 in its SEC filing.
The concerns come as a group of AI safety experts has criticised Anthropic in a new statement released in the days surrounding its IPO. Dubbed the “Misanthropic Statement”, it challenges the company’s claims about its commitment to developing safe AI.
“Anthropic is not a safe AI company, and we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good,” the statement said.

items.text:
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
- Published
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
'Recognition of our suffering'
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
