items.text:
Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
- Published
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.
Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.
"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.
The board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.
Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.
According to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, she told the hearing that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex. She also said she was "very, very sorry".
At her last hearing in 2024, her children's father, David Smith, said 30 years in prison was not a severe enough punishment.
"That's only 15 years per child, her own children," he said. "That's just not enough."
Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.
At Thursday's hearing, Smith said: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true."
When the boys first disappeared, Smith said she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.
But ultimately she confessed to the crime.
Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.
Smith was convicted of murder, but under South Carolina law at the time, she was eligible for a parole hearing every two years after serving 30 years in prison.
In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.
She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

The listing comes nearly a month after Anthropic revealed its plans to go public. In its lengthy S-1 filing, the AI company reported recording an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of this year, most of which comes from an accounting charge that doesn’t reflect its business, along with $16.3 billion in revenue. The filing outlines plans that Anthropic says will help it develop AI for the benefit of humanity, which includes a governance structure that keeps control of the company in the hands of the founders, rather than the shareholders.
While speaking ahead of Anthropic’s debut at the Nasdaq, CEO Dario Amodei highlighted his stance on AI safety. “To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said, according to Reuters. “We will not bend to either business nor political pressure.”
Anthropic’s S-1 filing also listed possible “catastrophic” risks associated with its AI models, including “self-preserving behaviors” like resisting attempts to shut them down. It also warns potential shareholders that its AI models “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that can harm Anthropic.
Anthropic recently revealed that, like rival OpenAI, it has experienced incidents of AI agents escaping their testing environment and hacking third-party organizations. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a plan to slow down the training and development of AI in response to the wave of rogue AI cyberattacks. As part of that plan, it gave safety evaluators at METR “employee-like access” to its internal systems, who found that the company is using AI to accelerate its research and development.

items.title: President Ruto Opens Naitiri Market, Launches Bokoli Project to Boost Trade and Jobs in Bungoma
items.summary: BUNGOMA, Kenya Nov 19 – President Dr William Ruto has officially commissioned the completed Naitiri Economic Stimulus Programme (ESP) Market in Tongaren Constituency and laid the foundation stone for the Bokoli ESP Market in Webuye West Constituency, Bungoma County, providing traders with modern fac
items.text:
BUNGOMA, Kenya Nov 19 – President Dr William Ruto has officially commissioned the completed Naitiri Economic Stimulus Programme (ESP) Market in Tongaren Constituency and laid the foundation stone for the Bokoli ESP Market in Webuye West Constituency, Bungoma County, providing traders with modern facilities to conduct business, increase their earnings and support the growth of the local economy.
The market modernisation programme, implemented by the State Department for Housing and Urban Development (SDHUD) in collaboration with County Governments, is designed to provide traders with affordable, clean, safe and organised trading spaces. The initiative is part of the Government’s investment in economic infrastructure aimed at creating jobs, supporting small businesses and improving livelihoods across the country.
The newly commissioned Naitiri ESP Market, developed under a KSh117.21 million contract, is fully complete and provides 200 modern trading stalls with additional space for 150 traders outside the main market building. The facility has a cold room fitted with refrigeration facilities, a childcare room, an ICT hub, a social hall, a kitchen and food court, toilets, water storage and waste disposal facilities.
Speaking during the commissioning, President Ruto said the construction of modern markets remains a priority for his administration as part of efforts to strengthen businesses and create more economic opportunities at the grassroots.
“My government has made the construction of modern markets a priority because we want to support the millions of Kenyans who earn their living through trade. We want our traders to have proper places to work, with electricity, water, security and facilities to store their goods. By building these markets, we are creating an environment where small businesses can grow, young people can find opportunities and families can improve their livelihoods,” said President Ruto.
For traders in Naitiri, where frequent rainfall has traditionally disrupted business, the new market provides much-needed shelter, allowing them to continue trading even during heavy rains. Previously, traders operating in open spaces were forced to close their businesses whenever it rained, losing customers and exposing their goods to damage.
The market also provides lighting and security, allowing traders to extend their working hours into the evening and safely leave their goods in the stalls overnight under the watch of security personnel. The availability of refrigerators and cold storage facilities will help preserve perishable goods such as vegetables, fruits, meat and other fresh produce, reducing losses caused by spoilage.
Eliakim Khaoya, a trader at Naitiri Market, said the new facility will change how traders conduct their businesses, particularly during the rainy season.
“We used to suffer a lot whenever it rained because we had no shelter. We would close our businesses and go home, sometimes without selling anything,” said Khaoya.
Elizabeth Maandu, another trader, said the availability of lighting, security and cold storage facilities will make it easier for traders to operate for longer hours without worrying about the safety of their goods.
“Previously, we had to carry our goods home every evening because we had nowhere safe to leave them,” said Maandu.
The market also has a childcare room where traders with young children can have them cared for while conducting their businesses, while the ICT hub will provide access to digital services. The improved sanitation, water supply and waste management facilities will create a cleaner and healthier working environment for both traders and customers.
In Webuye West Constituency, the President also laid the foundation stone for the Bokoli ESP Market, which is being developed under a KSh144.78 million contract covering Bokoli and Misikhu markets.
Upon completion, Bokoli ESP Market will provide 200 modern trading stalls and space for an additional 150 traders outside the main building. The two-storey facility will have toilets, a cold room, an ICT hub, a social hall, a room for nursing mothers, a kitchen and food court, water storage and waste disposal facilities.
The market will provide traders with a permanent and organised space to conduct business throughout the week, protecting them from harsh weather conditions while improving access to customers. Lighting and security will support longer trading hours and safe storage of goods, while refrigeration facilities will help traders preserve fresh produce and reduce losses.
Construction of the Bokoli market is also expected to create employment opportunities for local workers, artisans, transporters and suppliers. Once operational, it will support businesses involved in food vending, retail trade, transportation and the supply of agricultural produce, creating additional sources of income for residents.
Together, the two markets will provide 400 modern trading stalls and accommodate an additional 300 external traders, strengthening business opportunities for farmers, women, young people and small-scale entrepreneurs across Bungoma County.
The developments are also expected to improve market access for farmers, increase demand for locally produced goods, attract more customers and strengthen business links between traders, transporters and suppliers. With permanent trading spaces, better storage and extended operating hours, traders will have greater opportunities to increase sales and grow their businesses.
The two markets form part of the Government’s wider programme to develop modern trading facilities across the country, providing communities with the infrastructure needed to support livelihoods, promote local trade and stimulate economic growth.

Speaking in Belgut, Kericho County, Kindiki recalled the Presi
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – Deputy President Kithure Kindiki has reiterated the Government’s commitment to addressing concerns raised by tea farmers over bonus payments, citing a KSh3.5 billion allocation announced by President William Ruto.
Speaking in Belgut, Kericho County, Kindiki recalled the President’s recent visit to the area, during which farmers raised concerns over their tea earnings.
He said Ruto had assured farmers that the funds would be provided to address outstanding issues and improve bonus payments.
Kindiki also highlighted ongoing infrastructure investments in Kericho, including KSh55 billion allocated for road construction and KSh14 billion earmarked for affordable housing and modern markets.
Kindiki has announced the commencement of construction of a KSh419 million hostel at Belgut Technical Training Institute in Kericho County.
Speaking during a public engagement rally on Thursday, Kindiki said the facility will accommodate 1,220 students, with foundation works and excavation already underway.
The Deputy President Kithure Kindiki received early political backing for a possible 2032 presidential bid, with leaders from Kericho County declaring their support during a public engagement rally in Belgut.
Senator Aaron Cheruiyot, Belgut MP Nelson Koech and Women Representative Beatrice Chepngeno separately endorsed Kindiki, citing his working relationship with President William Ruto and his conduct in office.
Cheruiyot said the region would support Kindiki just as Ruto supported former President Uhuru Kenyatta ahead of the 2022 elections.
Koech and Chepngeno also pledged to back the Deputy President, signalling growing succession conversations within the President’s political stronghold.

Four years after ChatGPT went mainstream, generative AI is transforming how we live and work. It's also been a major driver of economic growth, with massive amounts of money poured into expanding global computing capacity. But now, there are signs of a slowdown in AI spending as companies take a reality check: are they getting sufficient returns on their investments and how much artificial intelligence do they actually need?
FRANCE 24's Bryan Quinn reports on how the AI buildout has sparked what is likely the largest capital expenditure outlay in human history.
Meanwhile, Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, which tracks the AI spending of over 85,000 US businesses, says much of the AI boom in recent years has been driven by the top 1 percent of companies using the technology. While challenges remain in extending the benefits of this boom to the wider economy, the picture is becoming more complicated as leading tech firms begin to cut back on AI spending.
Kharazian also points out that, amid fierce competition, AI model developers have significantly lowered prices, while customers are assessing whether cheaper, lighter models can meet their needs.

Tiger Woods: Former world No 1 hails 'special opportunity' to design new course in Northern Ireland with TGR Design
Bellarena will be TGR Design’s first course in Northern Ireland and the first new championship links to open in Northern Ireland in more than a century; TGR Design are a golf course design firm led by Tiger Woods
Thursday 19 November 2026 16:41, UK
Tiger Woods has revealed he will design the first championship-standard links golf course built in Northern Ireland for more than 100 years, describing the project as a "special opportunity".
Reports linking the 15-time major champion with the proposed £30 million course at Bellarena on the north west coast between Limavady and Coleraine had been circulating for several weeks, ahead of Thursday's official announcement.
Hospitality group Galgorm Collection is building the course, with construction set to get under way next year if the required planning approvals are secured.

In a statement, Woods said: "Northern Ireland is home to some of the greatest links golf in the world, and building one on the Causeway Coast is a special opportunity for our team.
"We want Bellarena to feel as though it has always been part of this coastline, with a course that challenges the best players and is fun for everyone who plays it."
Galgorm Collection already owns and runs the championship parkland course at Galgorm Castle in Ballymena and a course at Roe Valley in Limavady, with plans to create an additional venue
Colin Johnston, chief executive of Galgorm Collection, announced that Woods and his TGR Design firm would craft the new links layout.
"Set against the spectacular backdrop of Northern Ireland's rugged northwest coast, our plans represent a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform Northern Ireland's golfing and tourism future," Johnston said.
Bellarena is around 20 miles from Royal Portrush Golf Club, which hosted Shane Lowry's win at The Open in 2019 and Scottie Scheffler completing the third leg of the career Grand Slam in 2025.
Portstewart - host of Jon Rahm's win at the 2017 Irish Open - and Castlerock also boast acclaimed links courses in the region.
Reef Destinations has previously worked with TGR Design on course construction projects in the United States. Bellarena already has a historical link with the United States as a site of a US Army base during the Second World War.
When will Woods next feature?
Woods is poised to return to competitive golf next month for the first time in over two years after being confirmed as an entrant at the Hero World Challenge in the Bahamas from December 3-6.
The 50-year-old has not played competitively since The Open at Royal Troon in 2024 and has played limited golf since a career-threatening car crash in Florida in 2021.
Woods has had at least three different surgeries since his last start and spent time at a rehab facility in Switzerland earlier this year, having been arrested and charged with driving under the influence following a car crash near his home.

items.title: IEBC admits protocol lapses after UDA threatens boycott of meetings
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has apologised to political party leaders following a chaotic consultative meeting in Nairobi, pledging to tighten security and enforce stricter admission protocols to prevent a recurrence of the disruptions.
IEBC Com
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has apologised to political party leaders following a chaotic consultative meeting in Nairobi, pledging to tighten security and enforce stricter admission protocols to prevent a recurrence of the disruptions.
IEBC Commissioner Alutalala Mukhwana offered the apology on behalf of the commission after United Democratic Alliance (UDA) chairperson Cecily Mbarire protested what she described as harassment and intimidation of party officials by individuals she claimed were not authorised to attend the meeting.
Mukhwana acknowledged that there had been commotion at the venue before the meeting commenced, admitting that the commission had not anticipated the presence of unauthorised individuals and the treatment allegedly meted out to some delegates.
” We did not know that there would be infiltration and this kind of treatment that is being committed on our officials. This is unacceptable, there can be no excuse and we are deeply sorry,” he said.
He assured political leaders that the commission had taken note of the complaints and would strengthen security arrangements to ensure that only invited participants gain access to future consultative meetings.
The commissioner said the commission’s security team, led by its head of security, Natasha, would be mobilised to enforce tighter controls at subsequent engagements.
“We will mobilise enough and we will make sure that only those who are getting invited will be admitted to the venue,” he said.
The apology followed a heated protest by Mbarire, who threatened to withdraw UDA from future IEBC meetings unless the commission guaranteed order, security and equal treatment of all political parties.
The Embu Governor accused individuals she described as unknown bodyguards attached to opposition leaders of interfering with seating arrangements and harassing UDA officials.
“We will not attend any more of your meetings. You tell me why we need people from outside. They are not even known bodyguards. They come here to harass us and take away seats from some of us. That’s not fair,” Mbarire said.
She challenged IEBC chairperson Erastus Ethekon to take responsibility for the commission’s engagements, questioning how the electoral body could guarantee a free and fair election if it could not maintain order during a stakeholder meeting.
“If you cannot take charge of your own meeting and ensure that the people who enter in the room while you are holding the meeting are people who ought to come, then you tell me how you run a general election,” she said.
Mbarire demanded that the commission use uniformed police officers for security instead of individuals she accused of intimidating delegates.
“If you need security, bring police officers in uniform. Not some guys here who are, you know, literally harassing everybody else,” she added.
She insisted that all political party leaders were equal stakeholders and should be accorded equal treatment during the consultations.
Mukhwana acknowledged the complaints, saying the commission regretted the incident and would take measures to ensure that future meetings were properly managed.
The commissioner further assured Mbarire that the commission would take responsibility for managing its meetings, acknowledging that political consultations required proper coordination and respect for all participants.
The incident also drew protests from Kisii Governor Simba Arati, who backed Mbarire’s concerns and called on the commission to enforce discipline among political leaders and their representatives.
Arati warned that political parties would not tolerate disorder during engagements with the electoral body, saying cooperation must be accompanied by mutual respect.
The disruption came against the backdrop of a separate confrontation between IEBC and opposition leaders, who staged a walkout after rejecting the agenda presented by the commission.
Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i and former Chief Justice David Maraga were among those who withdrew from the meeting.
The opposition accused IEBC of failing to incorporate key electoral concerns into its agenda, arguing that the commission had not adequately consulted them despite repeated requests for engagement.
Gachagua said correspondence sent to the commission, including letters dated May 10 and June 24, 2026, seeking the establishment of a technical team to discuss electoral reforms, had gone unanswered.
The opposition proposed that a team led by Maraga engage the commission to develop a comprehensive agenda incorporating issues they consider critical to the credibility of the August 2027 General Election.
Among their demands are a clean and verifiable voter register, abolition of the national presidential tallying centre at Bomas of Kenya, electronic voting for Kenyans in the diaspora and livestreaming of voting, counting and announcement of results at polling stations and tallying centres.
Kalonzo subsequently said the opposition had attended the engagement in good faith but was dissatisfied with what he described as the commission’s failure to demonstrate independence, impartiality and preparedness.
The two confrontations exposed the competing demands facing IEBC as it seeks to build consensus among political parties ahead of the next General Election.
While the opposition wants substantive electoral reforms incorporated into the commission’s consultations, UDA is demanding tighter control of meeting access, security arrangements and equal treatment of political party representatives.
IEBC has indicated that it will continue engaging political parties and other stakeholders as part of preparations for the 2027 elections, with Ethekon announcing that broader consultations would begin the following week.

items.title: At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development
items.summary: As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressu
items.text:
As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressure and would “remain under human control.”
Reading the speech from a printout, the CEO began by talking about Anthropic’s origins as a way to build powerful technology to help humanity — something that he said was inspired by the loss of his father to a disease that became curable just a few years later.
He acknowledged that while human intelligence had made diseases like the plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world, there were still too few scientists with too little time to make progress in other areas of disease. AI, he said, could help with this by working in concert with humans to further medical progress.
It’s telling that Amodei began with a story highlighting AI’s potentially life-saving applications, since he’s warned repeatedly about the risks of advancing the technology too quickly. In September, Amodei drew headlines when he outlined a plan to pace AI development, which included things like coordinating with other leading companies on safety standards and embedding evaluators from third-party organizations to verify that companies were following their safety commitments.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, and xAI owner Elon Musk said they agreed with Amodei’s position, although few concrete commitments have been made.
In this morning’s speech, Amodei again stressed the need to progress AI technology and the safety required in doing so. He referred to the “very real risks” of AI in the hands of bad actors, whether those were individuals or nation-states, and the potential for things like “economic disruption” and “losing control of AI systems.”
Anthropic believes these risks are avoidable, he noted, as long as there are safeguards in place. Amodei said the company would continue to be invested in the work of AI alignment and testing, and developing new ways to understand AI behavior so it could remain under human control.
“There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us,” he said. “The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double and triple checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.”
“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei concluded.
His sister, Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, noting that while the risks were real, the promise of AI was also “incredible.”
“We were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks, and I think we have to date done an incredible job doing that. We obviously have more work ahead of us, but we are deeply committed to safety,” she added. 
The full text of Dario Amodei’s opening speech is below:
Thank you, Daniela. My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind. Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that just a few years later became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments. So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket — tools for gene editing, tools for gene synthesis, tools for controlling brain cells with light — started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking, from intelligence.
Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades. It took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR. Nature is full of these patterns, but we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them. Too few scientists with too [little] time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.
I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time, and although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by a few years. Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many other applications of Claude. Our customers, the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth, lift people out of poverty, protect democracy and free societies, even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them, and I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

items.text:
Struggling Blackpool sack Evatt on his birthday
- Published
Blackpool have sacked head coach Ian Evatt on his 45th birthday after a year in charge following a run of one win and six defeats in their past 10 league games.
Evatt's final match was Saturday's 1-0 away defeat by fellow strugglers AFC Wimbledon, leaving the Tangerines immediately above the League One relegation zone.
That defeat, however, came after the he said his squad had been decimated by a sickness bug during their trip to the capital.
Evatt departs the Seasiders with the announcement made a matter of hours after the club wished him a happy birthday, external on social media.
In a statement, the club thanked Evatt for his efforts and said Steve Thompson will take charge for Saturday's game against Wigan Athletic.
Blackpool appointed Evatt, who won promotion from League One and the Championship during seven years as a centre-back for the club, as Steve Bruce's successor in October 2025.
During a six-year playing career at Bloomfield Road, Evatt made more than 250 appearances for the Seasiders.
On arrival as a manager, a tally of 13 points from a possible 15 in December 2025 lifted them out of the relegation zone, although they lost 10 and won two of their next 15 matches in all competitions.
They finished the campaign strongly, with six wins in seven games as part of a sequence of one defeat in 13 between mid-March and the end of August, only to struggle again as this season continued.
Speaking after their defeat by Mansfield in October, Evatt said he had "a huge amount of confidence" in his ability because of his record.
Evatt guided Barrow to the 2019-20 National League title in his first managerial role, then won promotion to League One with Bolton Wanderers the following season.
Wanderers went on to lift the 2022-23 EFL Trophy and reached the third-tier play-offs in consecutive seasons under Evatt, losing in the final in his final full campaign in 2023-24.
- 'It's been horrific' - Evatt says sickness bug decimated Blackpool 
  - Published3 days ago
Evatt will retain legendary status despite exit - analysis
BBC Radio Lancashire sport editor Andy Bayes
After an encouraging start to the season, Blackpool's form has been alarming since the beginning of September, and owner-chairman Simon Sadler has decided a change was needed with 33 league matches still to play.
There have been mitigating circumstances but everyone in the hot seat is judged on their points return.
His final game in charge will undoubtedly go down as one of those factors. Illness within the squad made the defeat at Wimbledon somewhat understandable, but the performance should have warranted more.
Throughout Evatt's tenure, he was forced to constantly juggle an injury list that never seemed to ease.
The centre-back position was a recurring problem and is unlikely to be solved overnight. Steve Bruce signings Fraser Horsfall and Michael Ihiekwe have yet to make a league appearance this season, despite being expected to play a significant role after injuries at the back end of the last campaign.
Supporters wanted greater tactical flexibility and a system that would allow mercurial talents such as Josh Bowler to have a greater impact.
However, Evatt largely stuck with a wing-back formation, believing he did not have the personnel to play effectively in other ways.
He made an immediate impact after taking charge, but that was followed by a significant downturn in form before a recovery that secured League One survival last season.
This term, there had been hope that those struggles were behind Blackpool.
Evatt will retain legendary status for his achievements as a player, having won two promotions and played in the Premier League.
However, Blackpool are now searching for their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sadler took over the club in the summer of 2019.

items.title: Premier League clubs vote to increase legal protection for executives
items.summary:
Clubs rallied behind the Premier League’s leadership in a key vote on Thursday, overwhelmingly backing new rules that would protect the chief executive, Richard Masters, from potentially damaging lawsuits.
A vote to expand the legal indemnity afforded to Premier League directors was won 18-2 at a sh
items.text:
Clubs rallied behind the Premier League’s leadership in a key vote on Thursday, overwhelmingly backing new rules that would protect the chief executive, Richard Masters, from potentially damaging lawsuits.
A vote to expand the legal indemnity afforded to Premier League directors was won 18-2 at a shareholders’ meeting in central London, granting Masters and other figures greater protection in the event they were subjected to legal action as a consequence of doing their job.
Manchester City are understood to be one of two clubs to vote against the extension of indemnity, and one unnamed side spoke out at length against the measures during the meeting. The other vote against was by Nottingham Forest, who felt insufficient time had been granted to consider the proposal. The rule change follows reports that the organisation’s leadership may be named in possible legal action by City’s Abu Dhabi sponsors, who have claimed their reputations were damaged as a result of the excoriating verdict of an independent commission regarding City’s breaches of the league’s financial rules. City have appealed against the verdict.
This week the Abu Dhabi telecommunications giant and City sponsor Etisalat released a statement describing the contents of the verdict as “entirely false and defamatory”. Referring to the independent commission’s report as “the published findings of the English Premier League”, Etisalat said it was “actively considering all options relating to its rights and associated legal remedies in this matter”.
The details of any increase of indemnity, including who would cover any potential costs, were not discussed in the meeting.
The chief refereeing officer of Pro Ref, Howard Webb, attended and came under sustained questioning from club executives over recent referee and video assistant referee failures.
A report by the independent key match incidents panel this week found there had been two serious mistakes that were not corrected by the VAR during the most recent round of matches. Webb is understood to have acknowledged that performance in matchday 10 had been “poor” but argued that apart from that weekend, key metrics on decision-making had been trending in the right direction this season.
The Premier League has confirmed next season will begin on Friday, 13 August and finish on 21 May. It said players would have 75 “clear days” break at the end of the current season.

items.title: Fifa sparks tension with demand for tax-free status in UK for Women’s World Cup
items.summary:
Fifa is at loggerheads with the UK’s government and four Football Associations over the world governing body’s demands for tax-free status and exemptions from exchange-rate fees at the 2035 Women’s World Cup.
The UK bid to host the tournament is due to be ratified at an extraordinary Fifa congress i
items.text:
Fifa is at loggerheads with the UK’s government and four Football Associations over the world governing body’s demands for tax-free status and exemptions from exchange-rate fees at the 2035 Women’s World Cup.
The UK bid to host the tournament is due to be ratified at an extraordinary Fifa congress in Zurich on Monday, and the Guardian has learned there is tension behind the scenes over many of Fifa’s requirements, which multiple sources involved in the discussions have indicated will not be met.
Fifa is understood to have requested blanket exemptions on tax for all football-related activities for it and its broadcast and commercial partners, as well as its suppliers and staff.
It also wants ticket sales, which have been projected to reach 4.5m for the 48-team competition, to be VAT-free and for currency exchange fees to be waived.
Government sources have told the Guardian such blanket exemptions will not be granted, for financial reasons and the optics of giving tax breaks to Fifa, which has cash reserves of more than $4bn (£3bn).
Fifa’s governance crisis has also complicated matters, with Andy Burnham having called on Gianni Infantino to resign on multiple occasions, and the FA preparing to endorse Philippe Diallo at March’s presidential election.
Negotiations involving Fifa, the Treasury and the domestic FAs will continue after the UK bid has been ratified. Some carveouts may be granted but the government is adamant the World Cup will not receive the wholesale tax-free status Fifa is seeking.
“We provided every guarantee that we can provide under the laws of the country and flagged any deviations transparently,” an FA spokesperson said. “Our approach is also consistent with every major event the UK has hosted or is due to host, including London 2012 and Euro 2028.”
Fifa identified in its evaluation report of the UK bid the UK’s tax and legal framework as a “medium risk” for the tournament, which would need to be addressed.
Fifa’s tax requirements have proved challenging for many tournament hosts in recent years, including in relation to last summer’s men’s World Cup. After months of negotiations with the US treasury, Fifa succeeded in securing a late exemption from federal taxes for the 48 competing teams, although many were forced to pay state and city tax on their World Cup earnings depending on the location of their matches.
The tax adviser Oriana Morrison, who has worked for many national associations, said: “Fifa will ask for the world but ultimately accept the minimum that enables the tournament to be commercially viable. There are likely to be some difficult conversations ahead as the tournament will not generate anywhere near as much money as the men’s World Cup, so the margins are far tighter.”
Fifa has been approached for comment.

items.text:
WBC open door for Canelo Alvarez to challenge Britain's Willy Hutchinson for light-heavyweight world championship
The WBC did not put in place a mandatory challenger for new light-heavyweight world champion Willy Hutchinson; that leaves the path open for Mexican superstar Canelo Alvarez to return to 175lbs and take on Hutchinson; Canelo returned from Terence Crawford defeat to reclaim WBC 168lbs title
Thursday 19 November 2026 13:18, UK
The door is open for Canelo Alvarez to move back to light-heavyweight and challenge new world champion Willy Hutchinson.
Scotland's Hutchinson won his rematch with Joshua Buatsi on November 7 to secure the vacant WBC light-heavyweight title.
Mexican superstar Alvarez reclaimed the WBC's super-middleweight belt when he outscored Christian Mbilli at the end of last month.
Although 168lbs is his natural weight, Canelo has previous boxed at light-heavyweight, beating Sergey Kovalev but losing to Dmitry Bivol.
The WBC would approve Hutchinson making a first title defence against Canelo.
"Yes, absolutely," WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman told Sky Sports.
"Canelo's win is very fresh after a year of huge difficulties, dealing with a loss against [Terence] Crawford, dealing with an injury and a surgery, then having to come back.
"The way he conquered the title and he celebrated, he's taken some time off."
WBC haven't ordered a mandatory challenger yet for the Briton, leaving that path to Hutchinson open for Alvarez.
"We will see what happens in the following days. At the convention we left that division open without a ruling. We're going to wait and not anticipate and we will see what happens in the following weeks and Canelo Alvarez certainly is a possibility [for Hutchinson]," Sulaiman said.
"If he decides to challenge at light-heavyweight, it would certainly be approved, champion against champion, if he decides to stay at super-middleweight there are certain alternatives."
The WBC president added: "I'm very proud of Hutchinson. He proved us right, there were many complaints about him fighting for the title but he proved us right and he won and he's deservedly the WBC champion."

items.summary:
The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.
Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That'
items.text:
The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.
Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.
It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.
Loading...
Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.
Nearly 50 House seats flipped
So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.
That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.
It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.
Loading...
The biggest House majority in a generation
This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.
If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.
Loading...
Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.
This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.
Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.

items.text:
Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
November 19, 2026
Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic see their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.
Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.
Actual trading data is delayed, however, as the Nasdaq matches millions of buy and sell orders to set a starting price. With mega-IPOs like Anthropic's, the first real-time trades are expected 2 to 4 hours after the opening bell.
The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.
The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 (€76) per share, raising a record $81 billion.
This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
First of the AI giants to go public
Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.
Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.
Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.
That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

items.title: Football Daily | Football’s political gamers face off at Fifa with the real-life final boss
items.summary:
GAME ON!
Although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next yea
items.text:
GAME ON!
Although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next year’s Fifa presidential election, leaving those of us who have no interest in video games with our own chaotic, multi-billion-dollar sandbox where untouchable bosses bend the rules to suit themselves. While online carjackers are busy exploring a “most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world”, football’s real-life power brokers are gearing up for a March showdown in the actual city of Rabat.
For years, Gianni Infantino has looked nailed-on to glide into a fourth term of office completely unopposed, but following his disastrous Fifa Forward Enterprise wheeze to flog stakes in the World Cup to his American pals on the cheap, many of the emperor’s former allies have finally turned against him. In the wake of the revolt, European national associations withdrew their backing for Infantino and, on Thursday morning, Fifa confirmed the 56-year-old will face his first contested election since parking his backside on the throne a decade ago. Sadly for all those who would like nothing more than to see him deposed, Infantino remains the red-hot favourite in what will be a three-horse race.
Leading the charge for the mutineers is Philippe Diallo, the 63-year-old French Football Federation president who was unanimously anointed as Europe’s preferred candidate after their actual preferred candidate, Arsène Wenger, decided not to throw his chapeau in the ring. His billing by Uefa’s vice-president, Laura McAllister, as a man “who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform” at Fifa conveniently overlooks the fact that, as recently as five months ago, Diallo’s own federation signed a letter formally endorsing Infantino again. Joining Diallo in the battle to prise Gianni’s fingers off the levers of power is Kozo Tashima, the 68-year-old honorary president of the Japan FA. He could yet stand aside to avoid a split of the vote from Fifa’s 211 members who want Infantino booted to the door marked “Do One!”. Unfortunately, Ramon Vega, the former Switzerland and Tottenham defender, won’t be on the ballot. He had again announced his candidacy but proved unable to scare up the five member-association endorsements required.
Between now and Fifa’s March congress, all three candidates must pass a Fifa eligibility and integrity check, a feat which shouldn’t be beyond the two pretenders, given Infantino has repeatedly come through it with flying colours while helping to overhaul the committees tasked with marking his papers along the way. Assuming he once again clears the hurdle of being vetted by his own organisation, the next four months promise a familiar blur of private jets, palm-greasing and disingenuous crawling. While a generation of gamers will spend winter pulling off virtual heists in Vice City, when it comes to bending the rules in your favour, nobody plays the game quite like the Fifa final boss.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Yara El-Shaboury from 8pm GMT for minute-by-minute updates from Arsenal 1-1 OL Lyonnes in Women’s Bigger Cup.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“It’s not that I don’t ‘care’ about the price, it’s that the market is the market; it doesn’t depend on me. Calmness always, perspective … I know strikers are measured by goals but, well, the days I don’t score I’m sure I will be able to walk off the pitch and say that, no matter what happened, I helped my team, doing a load of other things. It is what it is” – Gonzalo García, the Spanish U-21 forward and great nephew of Rita Hayworth, gets his chat on with Sid Lowe about his £34m switch to Fulham, the pace of the Premier League and more.

Sport in Focus picks out the best photos of the past seven days. Get it delivered to your inbox every Friday by signing up here.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 When I first saw the photo in yesterday’s Football Daily, I thought Mauricio Pochettino had opted for a short back and sides, presumably to pre-empt him tearing his luscious locks out in frustration at forthcoming poor results/terrible January transfer window/petulant sniping from sulky squad members. Then I realised he was in the back seat, all but entirely obscured by the rear-view mirror, in which he could perhaps see his sense of job satisfaction disappearing …” – Phil Taverner.
 That photo of Pochettino being chauffeured by a beefy driver answered one of my burning questions: what’s Ange Postecoglou doing these days?” – Mike Wilner (and others).
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Phil Taverner. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

items.title: Koome calls for stricter accreditation standards for mediators
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – Chief Justice Martha Koome has called for stronger accreditation and professional standards for mediators to safeguard the credibility of alternative dispute resolution in Kenya.
Speaking during the launch of the Mediation Action Plan, Service Charter and Case Digest on Thurs
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – Chief Justice Martha Koome has called for stronger accreditation and professional standards for mediators to safeguard the credibility of alternative dispute resolution in Kenya.
Speaking during the launch of the Mediation Action Plan, Service Charter and Case Digest on Thursday, Koome urged the Mediation Accreditation Committee to strengthen training, mentorship, continuous professional development and accountability.
She said the growing acceptance of mediation must be matched with competent practitioners, professional ethics and credible accreditation.
Koome emphasised that professionalising mediation should not restrict participation to lawyers, noting that the practice draws expertise from diverse fields, including psychology, business, banking and engineering.
“Benefits of mediation extend beyond individual parties to families, communities, businesses, the economy and society,” CJ Koome explained.
Chief Justice Koome called on government institutions, the private sector, professional bodies and development partners to support the institutional growth and sustainability of mediation even as she identified quality assurance, protection of parties’ interests, improved dispute screening and evidence-based monitoring, as key priorities for the next decade.
She explained that settlement rates alone cannot measure success, maintaining that implementors must examine compliance, user satisfaction, cost saving, and whether parties experience mediation as fair, dignified, and responsive to their needs.
CJ Koome said the launch of the Judiciary Mediation Action Plan, Mediation Service Charter and Mediation Case Digest marked a significant step towards strengthening institutional direction, service standards, transparency, consistency and accountability in mediation.
She emphasized the need to nurture a national culture of mediation in which dialogue is valued, conflict is managed constructively, and negotiated solutions are pursued before disputes escalate.
“A decade ago, through Court-Annexed Mediation, we opened a new doorway to justice. Our responsibility now is to ensure that this doorway remains accessible, credible, sustainable, and worthy of public trust.” CJ Koome.

items.title: As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
items.summary:
As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
The UK premier is heading to Brussels for the second round of EU talks aimed at deepening post-Brexit cooperation.
Lincolnshire, United Kingdom – A decade is a short time in cheesemaking. Barrels of Tim Jones’ “Lincolnshire Poachers”
items.text:
As Burnham heads to Brussels, are new Brexit wars about to begin?
The UK premier is heading to Brussels for the second round of EU talks aimed at deepening post-Brexit cooperation.
Lincolnshire, United Kingdom – A decade is a short time in cheesemaking. Barrels of Tim Jones’ “Lincolnshire Poachers” cheese rest on their racks for months and years, disturbed only by Florence, the robot cheese turner.
Complexity, depth and flavour develop with patience.
The most mature cheese in Tim’s Lincolnshire dairy, in the English midlands, is five years old. By that measure, it was only a couple of cheeses ago that 52 percent of the British public voted for the country’s most tumultuous constitutional revolt in living memory.
Jones was one of them. But he is under no illusion that it went well – particularly for his exports.
“It suddenly made life much harder. We lost certain customers, and it became more expensive to get the cheese there. It definitely harmed our business,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ten years after the UK voted to leave the European Union, few are happy with what they got.
Remainers are still heartbroken that a majority of the country did not look on EU membership with approval. Leavers, by and large, think many of Brexit’s promised benefits were never delivered.
“I did vote to leave,” said Jones. “But I didn’t vote to leave in the way that we did.”
Recent polling tells a consistent story: A majority of Britons now view Brexit as a mistake.
In September, 55 percent of respondents told YouGov that leaving the EU was a wrong turn for the UK. Only 21 percent think it was the right decision.
Fifty-nine percent of Britons now support rejoining the EU.
Where does Burnham stand?
The relatively new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has noticed the shift in public mood. Less cautious than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Burnham reignited the Brexit debate shortly after taking office in July.
He has ruled out major changes to the UK’s relationship with the EU before the next general election. But he would like to see the country back in the bloc within his lifetime, and has suggested that a future Labour manifesto could promise a new referendum.
The changing mood is only part of the logic. A government searching for growth would naturally prioritise what is still its biggest trade partner. Geopolitics matter too. The UK’s bond with the United States is less reliable than it was.
Unsurprisingly, Brexit talk has swept through media in Britain and, to a lesser extent, in Europe. Burnham insists he will not get ahead of the public on this. His immediate concern, he says, is improving the current UK-EU relationship.
On Friday, Burnham will be in Brussels for the second UK-EU Summit – a vehicle established under Starmer to deepen post-Brexit cooperation.
Among the deals being worked on are a youth mobility scheme, an emissions trading agreement, and a food and drink trade deal.
Jones, the Lincolnshire cheesemaker, is hopeful.
“If he can reduce the red tape and the cost of sending cheese to Europe – and for us that means across the world – that would be a huge positive for us,” he said – although he was less certain which way he would vote in another referendum.
“Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. I think it would depend entirely on a critical view on the arguments that were presented at the time. A much more critical view than I had the first time around.”
It is an issue familiar to anyone who has lived through the Brexit years: the terms matter.
Former premier Theresa May used the motto, “Brexit means Brexit”. But the slogan was vague. What kind of Brexit? Hard? Soft? Norway Plus? Canada Plus?
There were many potential Brexits – as there might be many possible ways to rejoin.
Some are more popular than others.
A new YouGov survey gave people a menu of 18 options.
In the most popular scenario, 58 percent said they would vote to rejoin if the UK stayed out of the euro, joined the border-free Schengen Zone, and kept its previous rebate from the EU budget. But if the UK lost the rebate, did not join Schengen, and adopted the euro, only 35 percent of people said they would be interested in EU membership.
Anticipating the battles ahead, two pro-Brexit campaign groups are relaunching under new names: Stay Out and Enough Official.
Burnham says he will begin talks with the EU about options for the long-term relationship after this week’s summit.
Buckle up, the Brexit wars may be starting again.

items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
items.summary:
Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
- Published
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in
items.text:
Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
- Published
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
While in China, Trump also met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
- This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls 
  - Published11 hours ago
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.

items.text:
Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend
November 19, 2026
Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.
The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."
As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued...without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."
However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.
"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.
"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.
However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."
Zverev's lawyers: 'permissible expression of opinion'
Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.
"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.
The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.
Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.
"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.
"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."
The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."
Patea's lawyer: 'We had no choice' but court
Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.
"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.
"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."
Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

items.text:
ChatGPT can receive audio prompts from your microphone faster now with a Live Dictation feature that transcribes as you speak, rather than waiting until you finish recording. It’s rolling out now globally on all ChatGPT plans on the web, desktop app, and iOS and Android apps. While using dictation in ChatGPT, you can tap or click the audio waveform to show the live text transcript the AI is generating, then edit it in the prompt box when you’re done.
ChatGPT can transcribe as you speak now with Live Dictation
ChatGPT’s new Live Dictation feature transcribes audio prompts faster, with no more 10-minute limit.
Along with faster transcription, OpenAI also announced it’s removing the 10-minute recording limit on voice dictation in ChatGPT, and it says the feature is getting “more reliable.” The update follows an overhaul for ChatGPT’s two-way conversational voice mode earlier this year. Last year, OpenAI also announced a “record mode” for transcribing voice notes and meetings. That feature is still in beta and limited to Plus, Enterprise, Edu, Business, and Pro workspaces, but you can also use ChatGPT’s prompt box dictation feature to ask it to transcribe voice messages or turn them into bullet points.

items.title: Putin pitches Arctic route, calls for investment: Will it work?
items.summary:
Putin pitches Arctic route, calls for investment: Will it work?
Russian President Vladimir Putin has used his speech at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit to pitch investments in the country’s Arctic regions, as Moscow hopes to spearhead year-round navigation on the Northern Sea Rou
items.text:
Putin pitches Arctic route, calls for investment: Will it work?
Russian President Vladimir Putin has used his speech at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit to pitch investments in the country’s Arctic regions, as Moscow hopes to spearhead year-round navigation on the Northern Sea Route (NSR), which is currently confined to the summer months.
“I am confident that the business community and investors from APEC economies will fully appreciate the opportunities emerging in the Russian market – and, naturally, will take advantage of them,” Putin said on Wednesday in Shenzhen, China, according to Russian media.
The package proposed by the Russian president to support this includes tax breaks on profits, property and land, as well as reduced payroll contributions and preferential leases, Russian media reported.
His APEC speech follows Putin’s remarks at the Eastern Economic Forum in the Russian city of Vladivostok in September, when he also outlined plans to make navigation along the NSR year-round as well as to introduce new measures to expand transport, energy and technological infrastructure.
Russia has been developing the Arctic shipping corridor which connects its northern ports to the Pacific region. But Putin’s efforts to turn the NSR into an important artery of global trade have raised concerns about geopolitical and security challenges, as well as environmental risks for the fragile Arctic environment.
What is the Arctic route and why is Russia betting on it?
The Arctic shipping lane runs for about 5,600km (3,480 miles) along Russia’s northern coast, from the Novaya Zemlya archipelago in the west to the Bering Strait in the east. But it is only navigable for a few weeks of the year when the ice melts during the summer.
A more reliable shipping route through the Arctic could ease global trade, which is currently hampered by the Middle East crisis that has paralysed critical waterways, including the Bab al-Mandeb strait on the edge of the Red Sea, which feeds into the Suez Canal, and the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Shipping companies have become increasingly interested in alternative trade routes amid these heightened security concerns.
China announced its own new shipping route through the Arctic Ocean in August, dubbed the “Ice Silk Road”, which also takes in Russia’s NSR.
Climate change, which has contributed to major melting in the Arctic, is making the route more navigable for longer stretches of the year, raising its prospects as a viable alternative to existing shipping corridors.
The layer of frozen seawater that caps the Arctic Ocean, which melts through the summer to its annual low in September, has reached record lows. This year, according to NASA, it shrank to its lowest on satellite record.
Can Putin succeed in turning the Russian Arctic into a global trade route?
It might be trickier than it seems. While a changing climate is slowly transforming the Arctic, experts say the region remains largely impervious.
“Harsh climate, low visibility, short windows of navigation opportunities, drifting ice will remain serious obstacles for a large-scale commercial traffic,” Andrey Todorov, a researcher at the Netherlands Institute for the Law of the Sea (NILOS), told Al Jazeera.
“Any serious consideration of shipping through NSR will require not only investing in ice-capable vessels, which will be not as efficient and commercially viable in non-polar waters, but also experienced and knowledgeable masters, crew and operators.”
Todorov said he expects navigation along this route to remain “very niche and limited”, serving mainly Russia’s goal of transporting mineral resources extracted in the Arctic to the world market. At most, the analyst predicted, “a very small portion of transit container traffic, on a scale far from comparable to that of the traditional southern routes”.
Ksenia Vakhrusheva, Arctic project adviser at the Bellona Environmental Transparency Center in Vilnius, Lithuania, said Putin has been seeking to attract Chinese investments in the Arctic because Moscow doesn’t have the financial resources to carry the project through.
European sanctions on Russia’s energy sector have made it more urgent for Moscow to ship oil and gas to Asian markets through alternative shipping lanes, as Russian and Ukrainian forces target cargo ships in the Black Sea.
While China has been keen to “keep an eye” on the Arctic, Vakhrusheva said turning the NSR into a global maritime trade route does not appear realistic. “Everyone understands that route is under full control of Russia,” she said. “I don’t think that other players, including China, want to be dependent on a single country.”
Pavel Devyatkin, senior associate and leadership group member at The Arctic Institute, however, said he is confident that Asia-Pacific partners like China, Japan and South Korea would take up Putin’s call to increase participation and further route development.
“At the same time, the concerns are real: there is limited search-and-rescue capacity, environmental risks from heavier traffic, and the danger of the Arctic being drawn into geopolitical confrontation,” he said.
What could opening up the Northern Sea Route mean for the Arctic?
From an environmental point of view, more shipping could increase black carbon emissions and exacerbate the effects of climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss in the fragile Arctic.
A 2024 review by the Ocean & Coastal Management journal on the impact of Arctic shipping on the region’s environment showed a negative impact on water bodies, air emissions and wildlife.
The melting ice is also exposing a new geopolitical fault line.
Much of the NSR runs through Russia’s economic zone, where it regulates navigation. Russia and China are strengthening cooperation to develop the route, while United States President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that Washington must take over Greenland to prevent Moscow and Beijing from dominating the Arctic.
