Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the
items.text:
Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd
- Published
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."
Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.
The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.
He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.
The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.
Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.
So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?
There is a clear non-negotiable.
"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.
- Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino 
  - Published1 day ago
'Making the players feel like winners again'
It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.
Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.
United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.
One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.
"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.
"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.
"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."
Fixing a leaky defence
That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.
Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?
The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.
Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.
Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.
Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.
Then there is Dalot.
The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.
It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.
However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.
Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.
Solving the Fernandes issue
Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.
The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.
He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.
For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.
What else? Can any youngsters step up?
Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a £50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with £70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.
Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.

items.text:
EU targeted in an AI-assisted cyberattack, spokesperson says
November 19, 2026
The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was targeted by a cyberattack through the use of AI tools.
The incident was detected on October 22 and there was no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.
"This was an AI-generated cybercampaign," he added.
Regnier did not elaborate on the attack or name a perpetrator. He said the Commission "has taken the necessary steps in response."
This is the first time the bloc reported an AI-assisted cyberattack.
Disruption reportedly lasted 10 days
Regnier's statement came after Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission had been targeted. The report said the cyberattack disrupted several systems for 10 days and might have compromised large amounts of personal data. The European Commission has roughly 33,000 employees.
The Commission then convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents, according to Politico.
"We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. He also stated that they did not detect any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.
Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets, air traffic controllers, blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries among leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.
France summoned the Iranian ambassador last week over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test
items.summary:
Arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the company and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.
Amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes val
items.text:
Arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the company and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.
Amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes valued around a combined $307.9 billion at the company’s updated IPO price of $83 per share. Amazon, which invested $18 billion into the AI startup, would see its 14.7% stake hit upwards of $159 billion, while Google’s 13.7% stake is valued at nearly $149 billion, according to share ownership figures disclosed in Anthropic’s IPO prospectus.
A handful of other AI infrastructure providers are also positioned to benefit. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC have joined Google in committing $26 billion to Anthropic at its IPO price in a private placement.
In total, Google has invested $12.3 billion into Anthropic since 2023, with another promised $30 billion dependent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. And with the exception of TSMC, Anthropic has announced multi-billion-dollar strategic partnerships with its other infrastructure supplier investors — including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Microsoft, and Micron — that would see Anthropic purchasing their products.
This is the circular financing that has made some observers so skeptical of the AI boom. These companies are not just investors; they’re also Anthropic’s biggest suppliers. It might look like Amazon and Google are putting billions into Anthropic, but they get that money right back when Anthropic needs to train a model or serve Claude to users. From afar, it looks like unprecedented revenue growth for cloud companies and unprecedented fundraising from Anthropic — but it’s just the same money passing from one pocket to another.
Today’s IPO marks a critical change in that financing system, the moment it might just become self-sustaining. Those investments appear to have paid off, and are now liquid. Anthropic is still operating at a net loss of tens of billions of dollars each quarter — but it will no longer be suppliers and private investors footing the bill. Now, capital will come from a mix of public-market investors and corporate bonds, neither of which have the conflicts-of-interest that caused concerns before.
And critically, the company’s new bottom line looks pretty good.
Once it debuts, Anthropic is expected to have about $220 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, including proceeds from its IPO and the $26 billion private placement. Anthropic also has the ability to pay for future commitments in stock.
Joey Brookhart, who leads the Tokenomics team at SemiAnalysis, estimates that Anthropic needs roughly $280 billion in cumulative revenue over the next four years to pay for its compute bill, which Brookhart said is “achievable given where they will be next year from a revenue perspective.”
“The ownership stake is very worthwhile, and those companies no longer need any more support from [suppliers],” Brookhart told TechCrunch. “Amazon doesn’t need to prop them up anymore. The revenue is all coming from other customers.”
That doesn’t mean the server bills are going down, though. Anthropic has already committed to spend $900 billion, primarily for compute and infrastructure, according to a regulatory filing. Certain agreements have termination provisions, but Brookhart thinks the company is in a strong position to pay up.
On the other side, Anthropic generated $17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, putting the company on pace for a $68 billion annualized rate for the year. If Anthropic continues to grow at its current trajectory, Brookhart believes it could easily cover the gap needed to fund its compute.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, agreed.
“By the time the IPO is done, Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had,” Luria told TechCrunch, noting that the firm raised around $141 billion in capital and will take home around $91.7 billion in net proceeds at $83 per share. “And they’re not burning cash. They’re just going to have a war chest.”
A public listing will make Anthropic a more credible borrower, making it easier to raise money outside of public markets, says Brookhart. That’s despite recent reports that creditors might not see Anthropic as “investment-grade” material.
Luria distinguished between Anthropic’s supplier investments and neoclouds like CoreWeave, which he sees as more purely supported by circular financing. “CoreWeave wouldn’t exist if Nvidia didn’t prop them up, and it probably won’t exist if Nvidia doesn’t bail them out,” Luria said.
Brookhart also pushed back on describing Anthropic’s financing as purely circular, saying it was still “additive to the ecosystem.”
For both analysts, the biggest risk to Anthropic is simply that it will lose the AI race. Right now, the company’s growth is fueled by its status at the frontier of generative AI — but if it’s overtaken by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or even cheap open-weight models, that could change fast. As Luria put it: “If we’re all using other people’s models, then Anthropic’s not worth a trillion and a half dollars. It’s worth nothing.”
But regardless of who wins the frontier, compute suppliers will likely be just fine. Neither Brookhart nor Luria believe Anthropic’s growth is at risk, despite some arguments that cheaper tokens and more competition will directly affect the AI company’s bottom line.
“For Amazon and Google, the risk isn’t actually that high because in that scenario, we’re using other models,” Luria said. “I’m arguing we’re going to use a lot more AI. I don’t know if it’s all Anthropic’s AI….That’s still going to come from a data center managed by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.”

items.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
items.summary:
Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
items.text:
Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations with representatives from nearly 200 countries on issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
The text also includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that had been pushed by host Turkey.
It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries. But it did link the target to efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally alongside other energy efficiency measures.
'Little clarity' on climate financing
Another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether the funding should come in the form of grants or loans.
The second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion). It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.
Sandra Guzman, director of the regional network Climate Finance Group for Latin America and the Caribbean (GFLAC), welcomed the reference to tripling adaptation finance for developing countries, but said there was "little clarity in its implementation. Unfortunately, we are running out of time."
The text prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world."
"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.
What else is in the draft text?
The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.
It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."
Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand."
The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid and sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane. The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up — those technologies are as yet largely unproven at scale.
Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."
"It is actively more regressive, stripping out hard-won accountability, timelines, and legal anchors just as frontline communities in the Global South are paying the steepest price for climate breakdown," said Singh in a statement.
Talks in crunch time
The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run overtime. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.
Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.
On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demand for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate the potent greenhouse gas methane.
The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.
Bowen said he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.
"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming."
The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.
It's the first conference taking place with the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

items.title: Will Pochettino fix Manchester United? Will Unwin is answering your questions – live
items.summary:
Will is here!
Will Unwin is online now answering all your Manchester United questions. It’s not too late to get involved, ask yours here.
As Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge at Anfield, the Guardian’s Will Unwin is taking your questions on Manchester United’s new head coach,
items.text:
Will is here!
Will Unwin is online now answering all your Manchester United questions. It’s not too late to get involved, ask yours here.
As Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge at Anfield, the Guardian’s Will Unwin is taking your questions on Manchester United’s new head coach, the crisis he inherits and what comes next.
Ask a question: log in or sign up here
salfordexile66 asks: United follower since 1974. For the first time that I can remember I have no sense of optimism at the arrival of the new manager. Don’t get me wrong, I think he is a capable guy, but the manager isn’t the problem. It never has been since 2005. I feel that the only way to get the owners to quit is a full-on boycott of games by season ticket holders, ie leave just after the game starts and don’t return, coupled with ceasing to buy merchandise for the foreseeable future. What do you think?
Will: Fans are very loyal, and the badge of honour that comes with attending every game is a difficult one to shake, especially when clubs threaten to take away season tickets from those who don’t attend enough matches. United, and other clubs, know that.
United are bigger than a football club and have a plethora of revenue streams. They have been an underwhelming team in a big stadium for a long time, and their global fanbase has not been affected. But I do think one thing that would damage the product is swathes of empty seats at Old Trafford. It is a sports entertainment business at the Theatre of Dreams, and if the seats are empty, it becomes more depressing and harder to buy into. So a mass boycott would have a huge impact on the club.
Fan power has been decreasing with each passing year, which means bolder plans of action are needed. United supporters have done a fine job with their marches and banners, so it does feel as though they will eventually take further steps.
MademoiselleK asks: Do you think Pochettino will see Rashford as a key player in his plans, or want to bring in a replacement?
Will: Pochettino will certainly give Rashford every chance to prove himself. For the players it is a chance to start again but Rashford needs to show he can maintain professionalism and produce on the pitch. He is a quality player, who has the capabilities of being a gamechanger at the top level.
Pochettino will not write anyone off without giving him a go. Rashford had a decent season at Barcelona and has offered a glimpse or two since returning but without any notable output in terms of goals and assists. His contract is long and expensive, making him difficult to sell, so the player and club need it to work.
dNazareth asks: I remember reading that one of Sir Alex Ferguson’s greatest achievements was transitioning into more of a director-level role, allowing his assistants to implement their own ideas about how the team should play and modernise the tactics without losing the club’s identity. Is the director of football role the weakest link in Manchester United’s current hierarchy?
kiya asks along similar lines: Given how often Poch referred to himself as United’s “head coach” (a point of friction at Spurs), how often do you request interviews with the real power at the club – Wilcox, Berrada or Ratcliffe? What do you think of Wilcox and Berrada? Is it true they were appointed mainly on their success at Man City?
Will: I have written about the role of Jason Wilcox few times before. Martínez thrust him into the limelight in recent weeks, and he has faced the ire of fans, whose chants about the director of football have featured some choice language. The results on the pitch show there is a problem, but the blame has fallen on successive head coaches despite clear failings in how the squad has been recruited.
Wilcox desperately needs Pochettino to be the catalyst for success. Otherwise he will face a lot more questions, and may find his position untenable sooner rather than later. He had little experience of a senior first-team role before joining United, and little he has done since suggests he is capable of being a leadership figure at a Champions League club.
When it comes to signings, few come from outside the Premier League, which means United are always going to have to overpay. Brighton, who are second, have been built on clever scouting and data analysis, while United look at who did well at Brentford or Wolves the previous season. United need to change something about their recruitment, and someone like George Syrianos at Nottingham Forest, who thinks outside the box, would be worth considering.
Requests have been made to speak to Wilcox, but it feels like a futile gesture. As for the City connection, I think United saw the success there and wanted some of that influence.
Whosdatdandare asks: With Poch becoming the new fall guy who will get a tune out of the team before asking to be backed in the transfer market, being told we can’t afford player X and then leaving, how does the club remove the true issue? … So, how do you solve a problem like the Glazers and Ineos? No change of manager will do it.
Will: The fans point of view will be to remove the ownership, as they have made the case for. They are seen as a problem for numerous reasons, from taking money out of the club to moving fans out of their seats to make way for more lucrative hospitality clients. Nothing will really change at United until the team becomes the full focus and the right football brains are in the most significant jobs. With the current setup, the only way of things getting better is if there is constant success but the club is not built on such foundations.
Books have been written on the subject of United since the Glazers came to Old Trafford, so will offer some further reading:
We’ve had many questions about United’s finances. kapsiolaaaaa asks: Is there still the spending power to support Poch? Can United go out and buy a £70m player in January without selling someone? What about wages?

items.title: A geography of hearts: Turkiye and Lebanon, building the Levant together
items.summary:
A geography of hearts: Turkiye and Lebanon, building the Levant together
Some journeys feel less like a first visit and more like a homecoming. That is how I felt during my three days in Lebanon — my first ever visit to a country I had long known through its history, its poets and its people, but ha
items.text:
A geography of hearts: Turkiye and Lebanon, building the Levant together
Some journeys feel less like a first visit and more like a homecoming. That is how I felt during my three days in Lebanon — my first ever visit to a country I had long known through its history, its poets and its people, but had never walked through myself.
I came at the kind invitation of Dr Tarek Mitri, Deputy Prime Minister of Lebanon, who proved the most gracious of hosts. I came in a spirit of friendship and partnership, and I leave with gratitude. In every conversation — in Beirut, in Tripoli, in Akkar and beyond — I heard the same quiet determination: Lebanon wants to stand on its own feet, and it wants partners, not patrons.
I also leave with a full heart and, I must admit, a fuller stomach. From a za’atar breakfast on the road to Akkar to the sweets of Hallab in Tripoli and shawarma at Barbar in Beirut, Lebanese hospitality is everything people promise. Around shared tables, over strong coffee and long conversations, I was reminded that the bonds between our peoples were never only about diplomacy. Distance on a map tells you very little. What matters is the geography of hearts — and by that measure, Beirut and Istanbul have always been neighbours.
That warmth carries a responsibility, for friendship is proved not in words but in what we do together. Five convictions stayed with me throughout the visit.
1. Unity is Lebanon’s greatest strength
Lebanon’s diversity of faiths, communities and traditions is not a weakness to be managed; it is a richness to be protected. I was honoured to meet leaders from across the country’s political and spiritual life: President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and the veteran Speaker of Parliament, Nabih Berri; the Grand Mufti of the Lebanese Republic, Sheikh Abdul Latif Derian, and the Greek Orthodox Metropolitan of Beirut, His Eminence Elias Audi; Mrs Bahia Hariri, Vice President of the Future Movement; and Mr Walid Jumblatt, former leader of the Progressive Socialist Party. Different as their paths have been, each spoke of the same hope: a state that serves all its citizens, institutions that work and a future their children will not have to leave the country to find. National unity is the foundation on which everything else — security, recovery, prosperity — must be built. Turkiye’s interest is in a strong, whole and united Lebanon.
2. Lebanon’s decisions belong to the Lebanese
For too long, Lebanon has paid the price of being treated as an arena for the rivalries of others. That has to end. Nowhere is this felt more deeply than in the south, whose towns, farmland and families have borne the heaviest cost of this year’s war. Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity are not negotiable — and they must extend to every inch of its land. Occupation in the south must end, and the Lebanese state must be able to protect all of its citizens, from Beirut to the southern border. The choices about Lebanon’s future must be made in Beirut, by Lebanese, for Lebanese. Foreign states — near or far — should respect that. Real friends offer support when it is asked for and step back when it is not. That is the principle Turkiye seeks to live by.
3. A Levant-driven future, built on trade
The problems of our region will not be solved one capital at a time, and they will not be solved from outside. The Levant must think and act as a region, as it once did. The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus records that the Phoenician cities held their common council in Tripoli, gathering there to deliberate on matters of the greatest importance. More than 2,000 years later, our region urgently needs to recover that tradition of meeting, talking and deciding together, and Tripoli, which welcomed me so warmly, is a fitting place to begin. Our economies are natural complements: Lebanon’s entrepreneurial talent, its banking and services heritage and its ports; Turkiye’s manufacturing base, logistics networks and access to Europe and Central Asia. As Syria recovers, a corridor of trade, transport and energy linking our countries can become the backbone of a new regional economy. Let goods, investment and young people’s ideas move freely across our region, and stability will follow prosperity.
4. A record, not a promise
Turkiye does not come to Lebanon with new slogans; we come with a track record. We have stood behind UNIFIL’s peacekeeping mission in the south. Through TİKA and the Turkish Red Crescent, we have delivered humanitarian aid in Lebanon’s hardest hours. Now the task is to rebuild the south — its homes and schools, its hospitals and roads and its olive groves — so that every displaced family can return home with dignity. Turkiye stands ready to play its full part in that effort, and to help strengthen the Lebanese institutions that must lead it. We have consistently defended Lebanon’s sovereignty in every international forum, and we will continue to do so. Through the foundations and educational institutions I work with, we have seen firsthand how much Lebanese students and young people have to offer — and how much our two societies gain when they learn side by side.
5. Interdependence is not dependence
In a fragile world, no country prospers alone. Cooperation between Turkiye and Lebanon is not charity flowing in one direction; it is interdependence that strengthens both. When Lebanon is stable, Turkiye and the whole region are safer. When Lebanese businesses grow, Turkish businesses gain partners. When our universities, civil society and young people connect, both nations gain. The goal is a partnership of equals — one where each side brings its strengths and neither loses its independence.
The road ahead
I leave Lebanon convinced that the moment for deeper partnership is now. Lebanon has endured more than its share of war, economic hardship and loss — especially this year, and the south most of all. Yet what I saw was not a country defeated but a people ready to rebuild. Turkiye will

Man Utd latest financial results revealed as revenue and wages increase
Manchester United's latest financial results for the first fiscal quarter of 2027 covered three months up to September 30; it included the summer transfer window and their return to the Champions League, but not the sacking of Michael Carrick and arrival of Mauricio Pochettino
Thursday 19 November 2026 14:46, UK
Manchester United have released their latest financial results, with revenue and wages increasing.
The first quarter fiscal 2027 report covered three months up to September 30. It included the summer transfer window but not the sacking of Michael Carrick and subsequent hiring of Mauricio Pochettino.
It does include the club's return to the Champions League. However, only one of these matches were at home - a 4-0 win against Sabah. They played four further games at Old Trafford, and three away.

Manchester United's total revenues rose 4.1 per cent to £146.1m compared to the same period last year, while wages are up 8.6 per cent to £79.9m.
The club's loss after tax increased by 174.2 per cent to £18.1m, with interest paid down 32 per cent to £14.5m.
Non-current borrowings - the debts associated when the Glazer family bought the club 21 years ago - are up 19.2 per cent from $650m (£481.2m) to $775m (£577.4m), primarily as a result of refinancing. Current borrowings are down from £268m to £207.1m.
In terms of personnel, player sale profits down went down 54 per cent to £20.7m. The net expenditure on intangible assets - namely players - increased by £43.3m to £143.1m.
There was 17.7 per cent in broadcasting revenue - up from £29.9m to £35.2m - which likely coincides with Manchester United's return to the Champions League.
Matchday revenue is also up 2.3 per cent from £26.2m to £26.8m, although sponsorship revenue went down three per cent from £47m to £45.6m after the men's team had a smaller pre-season tour. Retail and merchandising also went up 3.5 per cent from £37.2m to £38.5m.
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada said of the results: "Our revenue remains strong and on track, while we continue to grow sustainably.
"We are pleased to welcome Mauricio Pochettino and his staff to the club and our priority is to support them as we look continuously to improve our performances on the pitch.
"We are pleased with the progress Eva Olid has made with our women's team and how well the team has adapted to her approach."

Somalia has ordered the United Arab Emirates (UAE) ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and withdrew its en
items.text:
Somalia expels UAE ambassador, accuses Abu Dhabi of violating sovereignty
Somalia says the UAE is interfering in its internal affairs with actions that amount to an ‘open invasion’.
Somalia has ordered the United Arab Emirates (UAE) ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and withdrew its envoy from Abu Dhabi.
Announcing the measures on Thursday, Somali officials accused the UAE of violations of Somalia’s sovereignty that amounted to an “open invasion”.
“Measures will be taken against anyone who cooperates with UAE in the invasion against Somalia,” Information Minister Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud said in a broadcast on the state-run news agency.
“All Somalis are urged to defend their country and unite against the open invasion of the UAE against the sovereignty, security, land and unity of Somalis,” he said.
Mohamud did not provide additional information on what provoked the expulsion.
There was no immediate response from the UAE foreign ministry.
On Tuesday, Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the UAE of giving economic and political support to regional Somali governments to oppose the federal government.
According to the Somalia National News Agency, Mohamud said Abu Dhabi signed agreements related to the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo with regional administrations and without the Federal Government.
He also said that the UAE helped to establish military bases and forces outside Somalia’s national command while the army is fighting the al-Shabab armed group and had given political and financial support that fuelled disputes inside the country.
The UAE, which has helped fund and train Somalia’s military in the past and has backed ports and other commercial ventures there, has long denied meddling in the country’s affairs.
Rising tensions
Expelling the UAE ambassador is the strongest measure Mogadishu has taken against Abu Dhabi since it annulled every agreement with the gulf state earlier this year.
In January, Somalia cancelled all agreements with the UAE, including port deals and defence and security cooperation, citing “harmful actions” that undermine the country’s unity and sovereignty.
The UAE has long leveraged its wealth to expand its influence across the Horn of Africa, using a mix of economic, military and diplomatic clout to assert regional power.
The UAE trained hundreds of Somali troops from 2014 to 2018, and still pays salaries and provides logistics for around 3,400 Somali military police and special forces troops in and around the capital, according to senior Somali sources.

Speaking during the first day of his Western Kenya tour, Ruto maintained that the po
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – President William Ruto has dismissed the opposition’s concerns over the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), saying the electoral body does not determine election outcomes.
Speaking during the first day of his Western Kenya tour, Ruto maintained that the power to elect leaders rests with Kenyans, challenging opposition leaders to focus on identifying a presidential candidate ahead of the 2027 General Election.
“The IEBC does not have the votes. The votes belong to the people.”
“First, you are busy struggling; find yourselves a candidate first. Imagine, up to now, you still do not have a candidate. You are moving from one hotel to another, from one person’s house to another, trying to find one. You are still struggling to agree on a candidate, and time is running out. After that, you will have to find an agenda and then start campaigning. We will defeat those people very early in the morning. These are the same people who have gone to pick a fight with the IEBC,” the President stated.
Ruto’s remarks comes hours after former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna on Thursday led opposition leaders in walking out of a consultative meeting with the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission after rejecting the agenda presented by the electoral body.
The leaders, who attended the meeting convened by IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, accused the commission of failing to incorporate critical electoral concerns raised by Kenyans and opposition political parties ahead of the August 2027 General Election.
Speaking before the walkout, the DCP Leader cited a letter dated May 10, 2026, reminding Ethekon of an earlier agreement to establish a technical team that would engage the commission on electoral reforms.

items.summary:
What the ICJ genocide ruling means for the Rohingya people
This is the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya minority ethnic group.
After seven years of deliberations
items.text:
What the ICJ genocide ruling means for the Rohingya people
This is the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya minority ethnic group.
After seven years of deliberations, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa delivered the long-awaited ruling on Thursday in a verdict which took three hours to read out.
Nine of the 15-judge panel found that Myanmar has committed genocide, the court said. Justices also voted in favour of a landmark reparations order against the country which it says has persecuted the mostly Muslim group for decades.
It is the first time in the history of the World Court, which was established in 1945, that it has ruled that a state has committed genocide. The decision is final and cannot be appealed.
The Gambia brought the landmark case against Myanmar in 2019.
After many years of persecution, Myanmar’s military launched an offensive in 2017 which forced about 750,000 Rohingya from their homes and lands, and pushed them into squalid refugee camps, largely in neighbouring Bangladesh.
About 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the early stages of the military operation. Thousands of others died in shipwrecks as they fled on perilous boat trips across the Bay of Bengal. The Rohingya reported cases of mass killings, torture and rape at the hands of the Myanmar military and allied militias.
“This is a huge day for the Rohingya people and all people of Myanmar,” said Matthew Smith, a campaigner with the advocacy group Fortify Rights, who nervously stood in The Hague’s Peace Palace along with Rohingya survivors and the Gambian delegation, as the ruling was read out.
“People have waited for such a long time for this moment,” he said.
The ruling “will provide much-needed momentum to efforts to hold the perpetrators and architects of the genocide individually criminally accountable”, he added.
Here’s what we know:
What has the court ruled?
The lengthy ruling, delivered by ICJ judge Yuji Iwasawa of Japan, said that Myanmar’s security forces “killed thousands of Rohingya” in Rakhine State, committed widespread sexual violence against them as well as acts of “extreme violence against children”.
Villages were “systematically destroyed”, replaced with permanent structures and then re-settled by non-Rohingya, the ruling said. The military also “intentionally” caused “serious bodily and mental harm” to the group’s members, and high-ranking officials disseminated anti-Rohingya hate speeches that portrayed them as “subhuman and a violent threat”.
Those who fled their homes have had little or no opportunity to return because of the destruction of their homes, the court found, and acts against children in particular established the military’s intent to “prevent birth” in the group.
Furthermore, the Myanmar military knew that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians and allied militias participated in the military campaign against the Rohingya. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” Iwasawa said.
The ICJ ruled that Myanmar must cease all acts of violence and investigate those culpable. Myanmar must also take immediate and effective steps to investigate all persons suspected of culpability, prosecute and punish the guilty, and provide guarantees that this will never happen again.
Importantly, the court ruled that Myanmar must institute restitution and reparations in the case – something campaigners have long pushed for.
Restitution measures, the court said, should see Myanmar: allow and facilitate the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; return or replace all collective property damaged; facilitate the search for the disappeared and ensure proper burials; provide for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured and ensure their protection from persecution.
The court said it could not determine compensation but ordered Myanmar to submit a report within two years outlining a plan.
“This judgement is a landmark victory for the Rohingya people and for countless individuals in Myanmar who have endured violence at the hands of the military. It represents an important step toward accountability and honours the courage and perseverance of the victims and survivors who have spent years seeking justice,” Arsalan Suleman, partner at legal firm Foley Hoag and lead counsel for The Gambia, said after the verdict was delivered.
For the Rohingya people, this is the day they have long hoped for.
“The Rohingya hope to receive justice and enjoy safety both inside and outside Myanmar,” Kyaw Min Sabber, founder of Rohingya Human Rights Initiative, told Al Jazeera ahead of the ruling.
“They also hope that they will no longer face displacement and arbitrary killings in Rakhine State,” he said.
Can the ICJ compel Myanmar to comply with this ruling?
The ICJ cannot enforce its rulings, but they do carry weight: The Gambia could now table the case at the United Nations Security Council and request action.
This ruling is especially significant because the 1948 Genocide Convention requires proof of the specific intent to destroy – in whole or in part – a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. That requirement is notoriously difficult to prove, and has contributed to the ICJ never having held a state responsible for committing genocide.
In 2007, for example, the court ruled that Serbia violated the Convention by failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops in Srebrenica but that the state itself did not commit the act – even though UN tribunals found individuals culpable for genocide.
Thursday’s ruling could, therefore, have important implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza.
Who are the Rohingya?
The Rohingya are a largely Muslim ethnic group based primarily in Myanmar’s western Rakhine State, which shares a border with Bangladesh.

items.title: Anthropic begins trading as $1.5 trillion company in biggest IPO on record
items.summary:
Anthropic begins trading as $1.5 trillion company in biggest IPO on record
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Thursday after pricing its IPO at $83 per share, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion and surpassing SpaceX as the largest initial public offering on record. The IPO
items.text:
Anthropic begins trading as $1.5 trillion company in biggest IPO on record
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Thursday after pricing its IPO at $83 per share, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion and surpassing SpaceX as the largest initial public offering on record. The IPO puts to the test Wall Street's faith in the AI boom, pitting promises of the technology as an economic game-changer against fears of a market bubble and risks to humanity.
Anthropic launched its blockbuster initial public offering on Thursday, smashing records and eclipsing SpaceX's June listing to become the largest IPO ever.
Buzz around its Wall Street debut juiced up beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq rising 1.96 percent a few minutes into trading.
The broad-based S&P 500 was up 1.1 percent, putting it on track to break a five-day losing streak, and the Dow Jones rose 0.5 percent.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei said the company's record-breaking stock market debut would strengthen both its finances and its commitment to acting responsibly.
“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said at the Nasdaq office in New York's Times Square, as Anthropic's shares began trading under the ticker “ANT”.
Read moreAnthropic files for mammoth IPO as revenues and losses mount
The company’s higher-than-anticipated pricing – at $83 per share – signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some market uncertainty stemming from the departure of Nvidia's CEO and worries about an AI bubble.
But the bigger test will be how Anthropic fares on the stock market.
Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by selling stockholders. Proceeds totaling $81 billion put Anthropic's IPO ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion in June.
SpaceX, however, holds a higher valuation, about $1.9 trillion as of Wednesday afternoon.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public.
Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Watch moreXi welcomes Trump: Does Nvidia scandal upend US-China AI race?
“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
The company’s rival, OpenAI, is not planning to go public until next year.
Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings as “substantial”. Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.
While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads.
Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.
Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.
Watch moreConcerns mount over artificial intelligence as Silicon Valley sees AI boom
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the US and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fuelled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.
Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centres. And two big states offering incentives for data centres, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction.

items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – The United Democratic Alliance (UDA) has threatened to boycott future consultative meetings convened by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), with party chairperson Cecily Mbarire accusing aides attached to opposition leaders of harassing government-ali
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – The United Democratic Alliance (UDA) has threatened to boycott future consultative meetings convened by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), with party chairperson Cecily Mbarire accusing aides attached to opposition leaders of harassing government-aligned delegates during Thursday’s engagement in Nairobi.
Mbarire protested what she described as intimidation and disruption by individuals she said were not recognised security officers, claiming they interfered with seating arrangements and subjected some UDA officials to unnecessary embarrassment.
The Embu Governor challenged IEBC chairperson Erastus Ethekon to take charge of the commission’s meetings and ensure that only authorised participants and security personnel were allowed into the venue.
“We will not attend any more of your meetings. You tell me why we need people from outside. They are not even known bodyguards. They come here to harass us and take away seats from some of us. That’s not fair,” Mbarire said.
She questioned how the commission could guarantee a free and fair General Election if it could not maintain order and protect participants during stakeholder consultations.
“If you cannot take charge of your own meeting and ensure that the people who enter the room while you are holding the meeting are people who ought to come, then you tell me how you run a general election,” she said.
Mbarire insisted that political parties attending the consultations should be treated equally, warning against what she termed preferential treatment of some leaders at the expense of others.
She demanded that IEBC rely on uniformed police officers for security instead of individuals she accused of harassing delegates.
“If you need security, bring police officers in uniform. Not some guys here who are, you know, literally harassing everybody else,” she said.
The UDA chairperson further warned that her party would not participate in future engagements unless the commission addressed the concerns and guaranteed equal treatment of all political stakeholders.
“I believe when we come here, we are equal as political party leaders. There’s no one who is more equal than the other in this meeting. Treat us as equal stakeholders in these meetings,” she added.
Her remarks came amid heightened tensions at the IEBC consultative meeting, which was also disrupted by a walkout staged by opposition leaders led by former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna.
The opposition leaders walked out after rejecting the agenda presented by the electoral commission, arguing that it failed to incorporate key electoral reforms and concerns they had raised on behalf of Kenyans ahead of the August 2027 General Election.
Gachagua accused the commission of failing to respond to repeated correspondence seeking structured engagement on electoral preparations, saying the opposition had been excluded from determining the issues to be discussed.
He cited letters dated May 10 and June 24, 2026, which he said had been sent to Ethekon but received no response.
The former Deputy President said the opposition could not participate in discussions that ignored concerns raised by the public and proposed that a team led by former Chief Justice David Maraga be allowed to engage IEBC officials in developing a more comprehensive agenda.
“We feel that any discussion that does not include those issues given to us by the people of Kenya would not be meaningful and will not be useful to the country,” Gachagua said.
He maintained that the opposition remained willing to engage the commission but wanted the outstanding concerns incorporated into the discussions, proposing that another meeting be scheduled as early as next week.
The walkout followed a meeting of opposition leaders under the People’s Coalition on Electoral Reforms, convened by Maraga alongside former Attorney General Justin Muturi and ODM’s Caroli Omondi.
During the meeting, the coalition outlined four major proposals it wants addressed before the next General Election.
They include cleaning up the voter register by eliminating duplicate, deceased and ineligible voters, abolishing the national presidential tallying centre at Bomas of Kenya, introducing electronic voting for Kenyans living abroad and making livestreaming of voting, counting and results announcements mandatory at polling stations and tallying centres.
The opposition wants presidential results declared at constituency tallying centres to be final, with the national centre at Bomas restricted to receiving, aggregating and announcing results already declared at constituency level.
Maraga said the proposals would form the basis of the coalition’s engagement with the electoral commission, arguing that the changes were necessary to strengthen transparency, accountability and public confidence in the electoral process.
The coalition also raised concerns about the independence of the commission, with leaders insisting that IEBC must be adequately prepared and insulated from political interference.
Thursday’s meeting had been convened by Ethekon as part of efforts to engage political parties and other stakeholders on preparations for the 2027 polls.
The IEBC chairperson had urged political leaders to cooperate with the commission, saying the electoral body intended to broaden consultations with stakeholders from the following week.
“We shall be meeting with all stakeholders from next week,” Ethekon said.
However, the rival complaints from UDA and opposition leaders exposed the challenges facing the commission as it seeks to build consensus among political players ahead of the elections.
While the opposition wants the commission to expand its agenda to accommodate substantive electoral reforms, UDA is demanding tighter control of meeting access, security arrangements and equal treatment of political party representatives.

items.summary:
Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.
With the biggest IPO of all time, An
items.text:
Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.
With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
Anthropic’s unusual power structure gives it free rein to shape AI’s future.
With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
Anthropic’s unusual power structure gives it free rein to shape AI’s future.
Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.
One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.
Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.”
The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi.
Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog.
Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.”
Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?”
Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement.
But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed nece

items.title: Joseph retains place as England change nine for All Blacks and drop Pollock
items.summary:
Nations Championship: Will Joseph retains England place vs New Zealand's All Blacks as Henry Pollock dropped amid nine changes
Steve Borthwick makes nine changes to England XV for visit of All Blacks in Nations Championship on Saturday (2.10pm); Fin Smith, George Furbank, Tommy Freeman, Seb Atkinson
items.text:
Nations Championship: Will Joseph retains England place vs New Zealand's All Blacks as Henry Pollock dropped amid nine changes
Steve Borthwick makes nine changes to England XV for visit of All Blacks in Nations Championship on Saturday (2.10pm); Fin Smith, George Furbank, Tommy Freeman, Seb Atkinson, Jamie George, Fin Baxter, Joe Heyes, Ollie Chessum, Ben Curry all return; Will Joseph keeps place on wing
Thursday 19 November 2026 14:00, UK
Will Joseph has retained his place on the wing for England's Nations Championship Test against New Zealand on Saturday, with Fin Smith among those restored and Henry Pollock dropped to the bench.
Joseph, who missed out on a place in England's matchday 23 for their 45-22 defeat of Australia a fortnight ago, started in last week's crushing 78-15 success over Japan, scoring five tries.
The 24-year-old picked up just his second Test cap in that victory at Twickenham, and his first since July 2022 under Eddie Jones. He moves from right to left wing for the visit of the All Blacks.
Elsewhere fly-half Smith, full-back George Furbank, wing Tommy Freeman, centre Seb Atkinson, hooker Jamie George, props Fin Baxter and Joe Heyes and back-rowers Ollie Chessum and Ben Curry all return as part of nine changes by Steve Borthwick.
Pollock, who made just his second Test start for England in 15 caps last week, drops down to the replacements bench.
Outside-centre Henry Slade, scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet, lock and captain Maro Itoje, second-row Alex Coles - who shifts back alongside Itoje from blindside flanker - and No 8 Ben Earl keep their places.
Alongside Pollock, the replacements bench is made up of hooker Luke Cowan-Dickie, loosehead Ellis Genge, tighthead Will Stuart, lock George Martin, back-row Greg Fisilau, scrum-half Ben Spencer and fly-half/full-back Marcus Smith.
"There are few bigger occasions in international rugby than facing New Zealand," said Borthwick.
"It's a fixture that always carries a special significance, and one that the players are hugely looking forward to.
"We know the quality New Zealand have in their team. We've prepared for the very best version of them, knowing the challenge they will bring and the level we'll need to reach to get the result we want."
England squad to face New Zealand in Nations Championship
England: 15 George Furbank, 14 Tommy Freeman, 13 Henry Slade, 12 Seb Atkinson, 11 Will Joseph, 10 Fin Smith, 9 Jack van Poortvliet; 1 Fin Baxter, 2 Jamie George, 3 Joe Heyes, 4 Maro Itoje, 5 Alex Coles, 6 Ollie Chessum, 7 Ben Curry, 8 Ben Earl.
Replacements: 16 Luke Cowan-Dickie, 17 Ellis Genge, 18 Will Stuart, 19 George Martin, 20 Greg Fisilau, 21 Henry Pollock, 22 Ben Spencer, 23 Marcus Smith.
All Blacks make eight changes for England clash
For the All Blacks, they have brought Codie Taylor back as captain and veteran Beauden Barrett is set to win his 150th cap as coach Dave Rennie makes eight changes.
Rennie has considerably strengthened the side after their upset loss to Wales last weekend, which left them one point ahead of South Africa in the Southern Hemisphere standings.
Taylor, who takes over from Barrett as skipper, is one of two changes in the front row for Saturday's clash. He replaces Asafo Aumua at hooker, and prop Ethan de Groot regains his berth at loosehead in place of George Bower.
Fabian Holland takes over from Josh Lord among the locks, while Tupou Vaa'i comes back for Anton Segner in the back row.
Damian McKenzie returns at fly-half and Cam Roigard at scrum-half, with last week's half-back pairing of Richie Mo'unga and Cortez Ratima dropping to the bench.
Jordie Barrett and Will Jordan return from injury among the backs, while centre Anton Lienert-Brown will earn his 100th cap.
New Zealand: 15 Beauden Barrett, 14 Will Jordan, 13 Anton Lienert-Brown, 12 Jordie Barrett, 11 Josh Moorby, 10 Damian McKenzie, 9 Cam Roigard; 1 Ethan de Groot, 2 Codie Taylor, 3 Fletcher Newell, 4 Scott Barrett, 5 Fabian Holland, 6 Tupou Vaa'i, 7 Peter Lakai, 8 Wallace Sititi.
Replacements: 16 Asafo Aumua, 17 George Bower, 18 Pasilio Tosi, 19 Anton Segner, 20 Leicester Fainga'anuku, 21 Cortez Ratima, 22 Richie Mo'unga, 23 Rieko Ioane.

items.title: Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere
items.summary: Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assi
items.text:
Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.
While some of the company’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year. With the new rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let users connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.
The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly does — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns users’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.
The productivity company is adding 20 new connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.
The company is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Users can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.
Until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. Users can also do enterprise search by using data from the company knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.
Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The company is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.
The company’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, said that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active users. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.
“One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants users to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.

items.text:
Germany's Wadephul: Berlin talks send strong signal to Moscow
November 19, 2026
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday's meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin sent a strong signal to Moscow that it was time to take negotiations to end the war in Ukraine seriously.
Speaking to DW during a visit to the South Caucasus, Wadephul described the summit as the largest meeting of Ukraine's supporters so far. The meeting represents the 18th set of high-level talks among the coalition's members.
He said it demonstrated that allies remained firmly behind Kyiv in the fifth year of Russia's war and were ready to do "what was necessary to ensure Ukraine could negotiate from a position of strength."
"The summit itself is already a success," he told DW.
Wadephul also welcomed the US initiative to restart peace negotiations. After nine months without progress, an initial meeting had taken place in Abu Dhabi, with a follow-up round planned and European participation expected.
Wadephul promises future support for Ukraine
"We are also preparing for the possibility that the negotiations will not be successful and that, over the coming winter, we will have to continue supplying Ukraine with heating, electricity and all essential supplies, including water," he said.
"And we will continue to stand by Ukraine militarily."
He stressed that any peace agreement must include security guarantees to protect Ukraine against future Russian attacks.
In earlier comments during his trip to the South Caucasus, Wadephul said that Ukraine and Europe must be involved in any negotiations over the future of Ukraine.
Wadephul did, however, welcome the trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
"Every conversation that takes place is a good conversation," he told DW during a visit to Azerbaijan on Wednesday.
Later on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said he had invited Europeans to Moscow for talks on the potential structure of future talks to end the war.

‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide – Cost of War
What happens when Israeli soldiers return from Gaza?
The film ‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide examines the psychological consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza through personal accounts of injury, grief and trauma by Israeli soldiers, alongside interviews with psychologists, journalists and Palestinian trauma specialists.
The film looks at the violence inflicted on Palestinians and asks how its consequences reach into Israeli families and society. Soldiers’ accounts of sleeplessness and fear sit alongside questions about military mental healthcare and the lasting effects of prolonged war.
Watch ‘Gaza Syndrome’: Israel’s Soldiers Haunted by Genocide, part of Cost of War, from Al Jazeera Originals.
